questions.text: At pH 9.0, in which form would lidocaine (a weak base with pKa 7.9) exist predominantly?
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: A weak base is mostly non-ionized when pH is above its pKa.
questions.modelAnswer: It would exist predominantly in the non-ionized form, because the pH of the medium (9.0) is higher (more basic) than the pKa of the drug.

questions.text: Define drug bioavailability.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Bioavailability = fraction reaching systemic circulation, measured as AUC(route)/AUC(IV).
questions.modelAnswer: Bioavailability is the percentage of a drug released from a formulation that reaches the systemic circulation and becomes available for biological effect. It is calculated by dividing the area under the curve (AUC) after a given route (e.g., oral) by the AUC after intravenous injection.

questions.text: Enumerate the factors affecting drug bioavailability.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: GIT absorption factors and first-pass metabolism determine bioavailability.
questions.modelAnswer: Bioavailability is affected by the factors that govern drug absorption from the GIT and by the first-pass effect.

questions.text: Explain why bioavailability of the IV route is 100%.
questions.explanation: Because no drug is lost to incomplete absorption or hepatic first-pass effect, the full administered dose is bioavailable.
questions.keyConcept: IV dosing has 100% bioavailability as it bypasses absorption and first-pass loss.
questions.modelAnswer: Intravenous administration delivers the entire dose directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing any first-pass metabolism or absorption barriers, so bioavailability is 100%.

questions.text: List the routes that bypass first-pass metabolism.
questions.explanation: These routes drain into the systemic circulation without passing through the portal vein and liver first, so the drug avoids hepatic first-pass metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Parenteral, lower rectal and sublingual routes avoid first-pass metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer: Parenteral routes (intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous), the lower third of the rectum, and sublingual administration bypass first-pass metabolism.

questions.text: Mention two routes of administration that avoid first-pass metabolism.
questions.explanation: These routes deliver drug directly into the systemic circulation or via venous drainage that bypasses the portal vein and liver, so the drug is not metabolised before reaching its target.
questions.keyConcept: Parenteral and sublingual routes bypass hepatic first-pass metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer: Parenteral routes (intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous) and sublingual administration both avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism.

questions.text: A main determinant of bioavailability following oral administration is:
questions.explanation: Oral bioavailability is chiefly determined by the hepatic extraction ratio (first-pass effect).
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic extraction ratio is the main determinant of oral bioavailability.

questions.text: A main determinant of bioavailability following oral administration is:
questions.explanation: The hepatic extraction ratio determines how much drug survives first-pass and reaches the circulation, making it a main determinant of oral bioavailability.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic extraction ratio is a key determinant of oral bioavailability.

questions.text: All of the following are incorrect regarding first-pass elimination except:
questions.explanation: Biliary excretion of drug by the liver is correct; metabolism does occur in the gut wall, first-pass does not change half-life, and it does not reduce Vd.
questions.keyConcept: The liver can excrete drugs into bile during first-pass.
options: Drug metabolism does not occur in the intestinal wall
Hepatic first-pass effect reduces elimination half-life
The liver may excrete the drug into the bile

questions.text: Drug A is acidic with pKa = 3, oral bioavailability = 70%, t½ = 6 hours, Css after 24-30 hours = 5 mg/L and Vd = 5 L/kg. As regards its oral bioavailability, it seems that:
questions.explanation: Oral bioavailability of 70% means 70% of the oral dose reaches the systemic circulation. The 30% lost is not necessarily inactivated in the intestine (may be first-pass), oral and IV doses differ, and the large Vd (5 L/kg) makes hemodialysis ineffective.
questions.keyConcept: Bioavailability is the fraction of an oral dose reaching the systemic circulation.
options: 30% of drug A is inactivated in the intestine
Its oral dose is the same as its intravenous dose
70% of drug A can be detected in the systemic circulation after oral administration
Hemodialysis is efficient in the treatment of drug A toxicity

questions.text: Drug A is basic and follows first-order kinetics. Its pKa is 9, its Vd is 300 L, and its clearance is hepatic. The following is true about drug A:
questions.explanation: A weak base is ionized and trapped in acidic urine, enhancing excretion; its large Vd (300 L) makes hemodialysis ineffective and it is better absorbed in the alkaline intestine.
questions.keyConcept: Acidic urine enhances excretion of basic drugs; high Vd resists dialysis.
options: It is better absorbed in the stomach
Hemodialysis can be used to treat its toxicity
Acidification of urine can enhance its excretion

questions.text: Drugs with variable bioavailability among different dosage forms are:
questions.explanation: Both digoxin and phenytoin are classic examples of drugs whose bioavailability varies between formulations, requiring brand consistency.
questions.keyConcept: Digoxin and phenytoin have formulation-dependent bioavailability.

questions.text: Important factor/s which may control diffusion of drugs across cell membranes:
questions.explanation: pKa, pH of the medium, lipid solubility and molecular weight all collectively determine the degree of ionisation and the rate at which a drug diffuses across membranes.
questions.keyConcept: Drug diffusion is controlled by pKa, medium pH, lipid solubility, and molecular weight together.

questions.text: Important factor(s) which may govern diffusion of drugs across cell membranes:
questions.explanation: pKa, pH of the medium, lipid solubility, and molecular weight all influence the diffusion of drugs across membranes.
questions.keyConcept: Diffusion depends on pKa, pH, lipid solubility, and molecular weight.

questions.text: Oral bioavailability of drug A is 60%; this means that:
questions.explanation: Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose reaching the systemic circulation unchanged, so 60% reaches the circulation.
questions.keyConcept: Bioavailability = fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation.
options: 40% of the orally administered drug is destroyed in the intestine
It should not be given orally
It is given intravenously in the same dose as the oral dose
About 60% of the oral dose reaches the systemic circulation

questions.text: The first-pass effect is most likely to occur if the drug is given:
questions.explanation: The oral route exposes the drug to hepatic portal first-pass metabolism; sublingual, rectal (partly), subcutaneous, and IV routes largely bypass it.
questions.keyConcept: Oral administration is subject to the greatest first-pass effect.

questions.text: The first-pass effect is most likely to occur if the drug is given:
questions.explanation: Oral drugs pass through the portal circulation to the liver before reaching systemic circulation, maximizing first-pass; sublingual absorption bypasses it.
questions.keyConcept: Oral administration maximizes first-pass metabolism.

questions.text: The following are true about diffusion of drugs across cell membranes except:
questions.explanation: Acidifying the urine keeps weak acids non-ionized, promoting reabsorption and reducing excretion, so this statement is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Acidic urine decreases excretion of weak acids.
options: Most drugs cross cell membranes primarily by passive diffusion
Acidification of urine hastens excretion of weakly acidic drugs
Aspirin is mostly non-ionized in the empty stomach

questions.text: The following are true concerning diffusion of drugs across cell membranes EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Acidification of urine keeps weak acids non-ionized, increasing reabsorption and DECREASING their excretion; alkalinization is needed to hasten weak-acid excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Acidic urine reabsorbs (does not excrete) weak acids.
options: Most drugs cross cell membranes primarily by passive diffusion
Diffusion is dependent on lipid solubility
Acidification of urine hastens excretion of weakly acidic drugs
Aspirin is mostly non-ionized in the empty stomach
Drugs can cross cell membranes mainly in the non-ionized form

questions.text: The following can affect drug bioavailability except:
questions.explanation: Plasma protein binding influences distribution, not the fraction of drug absorbed and reaching circulation, so it does not affect bioavailability.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma protein binding affects distribution, not bioavailability.
options: Interaction between drugs in the GIT

questions.text: The following conditions or drugs can increase the oral bioavailability of a lipophilic drug except:
questions.explanation: Enzyme inducers like phenytoin increase first-pass metabolism and therefore decrease bioavailability; the other options reduce first-pass and raise it.
questions.keyConcept: Enzyme inducers lower oral bioavailability.

questions.text: The following increases the rate of absorption of drugs:
questions.explanation: A decreased state of ionisation means more un-ionised, lipid-soluble drug, which is better absorbed. Larger size, lower lipid solubility and metabolism all reduce absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Less ionisation means more un-ionised drug and faster absorption.

questions.text: The following is a suitable route for irritant drugs:
questions.explanation: Irritant drugs are given intravenously; rapid dilution in the bloodstream avoids the pain and tissue necrosis seen with IM or SC injection.
questions.keyConcept: Irritant/sclerosant drugs should be given intravenously to avoid local tissue injury.

questions.text: The following is a suitable route for irritant drugs:
questions.explanation: Irritant drugs are best given IV, where rapid dilution in blood minimizes tissue irritation; SC and IM cause pain and necrosis.
questions.keyConcept: Irritant drugs are given IV to avoid tissue damage.

questions.text: The following is true concerning diffusion of drugs across cell membranes:
questions.explanation: Passive diffusion, the main route for most drugs, depends on a drug's lipid solubility. Acidification of urine reduces excretion of weak acids, weak acids are non-ionised in the acidic stomach (not alkaline intestine), and drugs cross mainly in the un-ionised form.
questions.keyConcept: Lipid solubility governs passive diffusion of drugs across membranes.
options: Most drugs cross cell membranes primarily by facilitated diffusion.
Acidification of urine increases excretion of weakly acidic drugs.
Aspirin (acid) is mostly non-ionised in the alkaline medium of intestine.
Drugs can cross cell membrane mainly in an ionised form.

questions.text: The following is true concerning drug diffusion across cell membranes EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Acidification of urine reduces (does not hasten) excretion of weak acids by promoting their reabsorption. The other statements are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Acidifying urine traps and reabsorbs weak acids, reducing their excretion.
options: Most drugs cross cell membranes primarily by passive diffusion.
Acidification of urine hastens excretion of weakly acidic drugs.
Aspirin is mostly non-ionised in the empty stomach.
Drugs can cross cell membrane mainly in un-ionised form.

questions.text: The following route is used only for topical administration:
questions.explanation: The skin route is essentially topical/local; inhalation, intranasal, and rectal routes can achieve systemic absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Skin application is a purely topical route.

questions.text: The following route is used only for topical drug administration:
questions.explanation: None of these routes is exclusively topical: skin (transdermal patches), inhalation, intranasal, and rectal routes can each achieve systemic absorption in addition to local effects.
questions.keyConcept: Skin, inhalation, intranasal, and rectal routes can all produce systemic effects.

questions.text: The following route(s) of administration is/are suitable for systemic drug administration:
questions.explanation: Intranasal, inhalational, intravenous and transdermal routes can all deliver drugs into the systemic circulation.
questions.keyConcept: Many routes (IN, inhaled, IV, transdermal) achieve systemic delivery.

questions.text: Which of the following does not affect oral bioavailability:
questions.explanation: Elimination half-life is an elimination parameter and does not influence the fraction of drug reaching the systemic circulation (oral bioavailability).
questions.keyConcept: Elimination half-life does not determine oral bioavailability.
options: Fraction of the drug absorbed from intestine.
Metabolism of drugs in wall of intestine and in the liver.

questions.text: Which of the following factors increases absorption of a drug?
questions.explanation: Increased lipophilicity enhances passive diffusion and absorption. Ionisation, loss of absorptive surface, food, and gastric instability all reduce absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Greater lipophilicity increases drug absorption across membranes.
options: Surgical resection of part of the GIT
Instability of the drug in gastric HCl

questions.text: Which of the following is/are true?
questions.explanation: Hepatic extraction governs oral bioavailability and digoxin/phenytoin have variable bioavailability (A and D true). Dialysis is ineffective for high-Vd drugs and propranolol saturates/reduces first-pass metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Oral bioavailability depends on hepatic extraction; digoxin/phenytoin vary.
options: Bioavailability after oral administration is determined by hepatic extraction
Dialysis is useful in toxicity of drugs with large Vd
Drugs with variable bioavailability include digoxin and phenytoin

questions.text: Which of the following is true about an acidic drug?
questions.explanation: In alkaline urine a weak acid becomes ionized and is trapped, enhancing its excretion; pKa is constant and an acid is non-ionized (well absorbed) in the acidic stomach.
questions.keyConcept: Alkaline urine enhances excretion of acidic drugs.
options: pKa will increase in acidic media
It is highly ionized in the stomach
It is better absorbed in the intestine
Alkalinization of urine can help in its excretion

questions.text: Which of the following is true about oral dosage forms?
questions.explanation: A spansule is a sustained-release capsule containing immediate-release plus slow-release pellets, giving both rapid onset and prolonged duration. An enteric-coated (not merely "coated") tablet dissolves in the intestine; a syrup is a concentrated sugar solution; an elixir is a sweetened hydro-alcoholic (not purely aqueous) solution.
questions.keyConcept: A spansule combines immediate- and sustained-release pellets for rapid onset with long duration.
options: Coated tablet / coat dissolves in the intestine to avoid gastric irritation
Syrup / aqueous solution of the drug
Spansule / has rapid onset and long duration
Elixir / sweetened aqueous solution of the drug

questions.text: Which of the following routes favors patient compliance the most?
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous implants (depot preparations) release drug slowly over weeks to months, requiring infrequent administration and maximizing compliance.
questions.keyConcept: Long-acting depot/implant preparations improve compliance by reducing dosing frequency.

questions.text: Which of the following routes of administration allows for titrating the dose of a drug with the response?
questions.explanation: Slow IV infusion and inhalation allow moment-to-moment titration of dose against response; transdermal and sublingual routes do not.
questions.keyConcept: IV infusion and inhalation allow titration of dose to response.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are True?
questions.explanation: Oral bioavailability is largely set by the hepatic extraction ratio, and digoxin and phenytoin are classic drugs with variable bioavailability. Dialysis fails with large Vd, and propranolol decreases first-pass metabolism by reducing hepatic blood flow.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic extraction ratio determines oral bioavailability; digoxin/phenytoin vary.
options: Oral bioavailability is determined by hepatic extraction ratio.
Dialysis is useful in toxicity of drugs with large volume of distribution.
Propranolol increases hepatic first pass metabolism.
Drugs with variable bioavailability include digoxin and phenytoin.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is true?
questions.explanation: Increasing polarity reduces tubular reabsorption and enhances renal excretion. Lipid solubility decreases excretion, urine alkalinisation increases weak-acid excretion, and an alkaline medium ionises weak acids reducing their absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Increasing a drug's polarity enhances its renal excretion.
options: Lipid solubility increases renal excretion of drugs.
Urine alkalinisation decreases the excretion of weak acids.
Addition of bicarbonate (alkali) increases the absorption of weak acids.
Excretion is enhanced by increasing polarity.
Alkaline medium of intestine enhances absorption of weak acidic drugs.

questions.text: Define volume of distribution.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Vd is the apparent volume relating total body drug to plasma concentration.
questions.modelAnswer: The volume of distribution is the volume that would accommodate the entire amount of drug in the body if its concentration throughout the body were the same as that in plasma.

questions.text: Describe what the volume of distribution indicates about the extent of tissue uptake of drugs.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Small Vd = limited tissue uptake; large Vd = extensive distribution.
questions.modelAnswer: A small Vd (e.g., frusemide) indicates that tissue uptake is limited, whereas a large Vd (e.g., digoxin) indicates extensive tissue distribution.

questions.text: Discuss the clinical significance of binding to plasma protein.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Protein binding lowers free drug, prolongs half-life and underlies displacement interactions.
questions.modelAnswer: Plasma protein binding facilitates drug absorption by keeping the free plasma concentration low, limits tissue penetration and decreases the volume of distribution. The bound fraction cannot be eliminated and acts as a reservoir that continuously releases free drug, prolonging the half-life. Heavy binding can make the free level too low to be effective against dangerous infections, and drugs sharing the acidic (low-capacity) binding site of albumin can displace one another, causing clinically significant drug interactions.

questions.text: Discuss the clinical significance of determining the volume of distribution of drugs.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Vd predicts tissue uptake, dialysis usefulness and the loading dose.
questions.modelAnswer: Vd estimates the extent of tissue uptake of a drug. In toxicity, dialysis is not useful for high-Vd drugs (most drug is in the tissues) but is useful for low-Vd drugs (most drug is in blood and extracellular fluid). Vd is also used to calculate the loading dose.

questions.text: Explain why aspirin may increase the risk of toxicity with warfarin.
questions.explanation: Both drugs are highly protein bound; displacement raises the free warfarin fraction, enhancing its anticoagulant effect and bleeding risk.
questions.keyConcept: Aspirin displaces protein-bound warfarin, increasing free drug and bleeding.
questions.modelAnswer: Aspirin displaces warfarin from plasma protein binding sites, increasing free active warfarin and raising the risk of toxicity and bleeding.

questions.text: Explain why dialysis is not used with high Vd drugs.
questions.explanation: Dialysis can only clear drug present in the blood compartment, so when most of the drug is in tissues a large Vd renders dialysis useless.
questions.keyConcept: High Vd drugs are poorly dialysable because little drug stays in plasma.
questions.modelAnswer: Drugs with a high volume of distribution are extensively distributed into body tissues, leaving little drug in the plasma; since dialysis removes drug from plasma, it is ineffective.

questions.text: Explain why dialysis is not used with high volume-of-distribution drugs.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: High Vd leaves little drug in plasma for dialysis to remove.
questions.modelAnswer: High-Vd drugs are taken up extensively into the tissues, so only a small amount remains in the plasma available to be removed by dialysis.

questions.text: Explain why tetracyclines are contraindicated in a pregnant woman.
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines bind calcium in developing mineralised tissues, so transplacental exposure damages the foetal skeleton and dentition.
questions.keyConcept: Tetracyclines chelate calcium and harm foetal bone and teeth.
questions.modelAnswer: Tetracyclines chelate calcium and deposit in foetal bone and teeth, causing permanent teeth discolouration and impaired bone growth.

questions.text: List four factors affecting the volume of distribution.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Perfusion, diffusion, protein binding and tissue binding determine Vd.
questions.modelAnswer: Factors include perfusion, diffusion, plasma protein binding, binding to tissue constituents and capillary permeability.

questions.text: List the pharmacokinetic characteristics of a drug with high lipid solubility.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Lipophilic drugs are well absorbed, widely distributed, hepatically cleared and reabsorbed renally.
questions.modelAnswer: High lipophilicity facilitates absorption, increases the volume of distribution (the drug penetrates most tissues including CNS and placenta and enters cells), increases hepatic elimination (the drug enters hepatocytes) and decreases renal excretion (due to increased tubular reabsorption).

questions.text: List the pharmacokinetic properties of a drug of which more than 90% of the dose is bound to plasma protein.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Highly protein-bound drugs have small Vd, long half-life and limited free fraction.
questions.modelAnswer: Such a drug has facilitated absorption due to a low free plasma concentration, limited tissue penetration with a decreased volume of distribution, and a bound reservoir that continuously releases free drug and prolongs the half-life. The free level may be too low to be effective against dangerous infections.

questions.text: Mention how the loading dose can be calculated.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Loading dose = Vd x Css.
questions.modelAnswer: The loading dose equals the volume of distribution multiplied by the desired steady-state plasma concentration: LD = Vd x Css.

questions.text: A 25-year-old woman was admitted after ingesting 50 tablets of drug X (total dose 2000 mg). Investigations revealed a serum drug level of 10 mg/L. The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) of drug X is:
questions.explanation: Vd = dose / plasma concentration = 2000 mg / 10 mg/L = 200 L.
questions.keyConcept: Vd = dose / plasma concentration.

questions.text: A 36-year-old man diagnosed with malaria received 600 mg of hydroxychloroquine (3 tablets) as a loading dose. The peak plasma concentration was 0.05 mg/L. The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is:
questions.explanation: Vd = dose / plasma concentration = 600 mg / 0.05 mg/L = 12000 L, reflecting extensive tissue binding.
questions.keyConcept: Very low plasma concentration gives a very large Vd.

questions.text: A 40-year-old man with a methicillin-resistant S. aureus infection received 2000 mg of vancomycin as an IV loading dose. The peak plasma concentration was 28.5 mg/L. The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is:
questions.explanation: Vd = dose / plasma concentration = 2000 mg / 28.5 mg/L = ~70 L.
questions.keyConcept: Vd = dose / plasma concentration.

questions.text: A high Vd for a drug indicates which of the following effect:
questions.explanation: A high Vd reflects extensive tissue distribution, which is characteristic of highly lipophilic drugs.
questions.keyConcept: A high Vd signals extensive tissue distribution of lipophilic drugs.
options: Many receptors for the molecules are available.

questions.text: All the following regarding binding of drugs to plasma protein are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: It is aspirin that displaces warfarin from plasma protein (increasing free warfarin and bleeding risk), not the reverse.
questions.keyConcept: Aspirin displaces warfarin from albumin, increasing bleeding risk.
options: Binding facilitates drug absorption by keeping the concentration gradient.
Drug binding to albumin can displace each other leading to clinically significant interaction when the drug is highly bound.
Binding to plasma protein lowers Vd of drugs.
Warfarin can displace aspirin from binding to plasma protein.

questions.text: Choose the correct answer:
questions.explanation: Systemic clearance equals the sum of all individual organ clearances (renal, hepatic, etc.). Weak bases are absorbed in the intestine, large Vd resists dialysis, atropine slows gastric emptying, and small Vd means drug is mostly in plasma.
questions.keyConcept: Systemic clearance is the sum of individual organ clearances.
options: Weak bases are absorbed efficiently across gastric mucosa.
Drugs with large Vd can be removed effectively by haemodialysis.
Cls (systemic clearance) is the sum of individual organ clearances.
Co-administration of atropine speeds absorption of all drugs.
If Vd of a drug is small, most of the drug is in intracellular space.

questions.text: Choose the correct answer regarding binding to plasma protein:
questions.explanation: If extensive binding leaves too little free drug, effective concentrations may not be reached for serious infections. Only the free form is active, binding limits tissue uptake, and displacement is dangerous for low-Vd highly bound drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Excessive protein binding can leave too little free drug to be effective.
options: Bound form is the only active part of the drug.
High binding to plasma protein increases tissue uptake.
Displacement of drugs from plasma protein induces serious adverse effects with drugs that have high Vd.
Drugs with too low a free part are not effective against dangerous infection.

questions.text: Drug distribution is not affected by:
questions.explanation: Clearance is an elimination parameter and does not directly affect how a drug distributes; pH, blood flow and protein binding all influence distribution.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance governs elimination, not distribution.

questions.text: Drug distribution is not affected by:
questions.explanation: Drug clearance relates to elimination and does not affect distribution; pH, blood flow, protein binding and lipid solubility all do.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance is an elimination parameter, unrelated to distribution.

questions.text: Drug X has Vd = 39 L in a patient weighing 70 kg. The extent of its distribution is nearly:
questions.explanation: A Vd of about 39 L (around 0.5-0.6 L/kg) corresponds to distribution throughout total body water.
questions.keyConcept: A Vd near 0.6 L/kg indicates distribution in total body water.

questions.text: Drug X is given in a dose of 500 mg to a woman with a body weight of 100 kg until Cp was 100 mg/dl. The drug is mainly present in:
questions.explanation: Cp of 100 mg/dl equals 1000 mg/L, giving Vd = 500/1000 = 0.5 L, far below plasma volume, so the drug is confined to plasma.
questions.keyConcept: A very small Vd means the drug stays in plasma.

questions.text: Drugs binding to plasma protein have the following features except:
questions.explanation: Plasma protein binding acts as a reservoir and prolongs (not shortens) the elimination half-life, so this statement is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Protein binding prolongs elimination half-life.
options: Binding facilitates drug absorption by decreasing its free concentration
Binding limits tissue penetration and decreases Vd
Binding decreases the free fraction, which is ineffective in treating dangerous infections

questions.text: Drugs with a small volume of distribution are characterized by:
questions.explanation: A small Vd means the drug stays in plasma (limited tissue uptake), so dialysis is effective, and Vd cannot fall below the plasma volume (~3.5 L).
questions.keyConcept: Small Vd drugs stay in plasma and are dialyzable.
options: Their Vd cannot be less than 3.5 liters

questions.text: Drugs with a small volume of distribution (Vd) are characterised by:
questions.explanation: A small Vd reflects limited tissue uptake with the drug largely confined to plasma (about 4-5 L), so haemodialysis is effective in toxicity. All three statements apply.
questions.keyConcept: A small Vd keeps drug in plasma, making dialysis useful in toxicity.

questions.text: Lipophilicity reduces:
questions.explanation: Lipophilic drugs are reabsorbed in the renal tubules, so lipophilicity reduces renal excretion (they must be metabolized first). It increases absorption and Vd.
questions.keyConcept: Lipophilicity decreases renal excretion (promotes tubular reabsorption).

questions.text: Regarding pharmacokinetics, all of the following are correct except:
questions.explanation: Vd is an apparent volume and can far exceed total body water when a drug distributes extensively into tissues such as fat. The other statements are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Apparent Vd can exceed total body water with extensive tissue uptake.
options: Vd is the ratio between total dose of a drug in the body and its Cp.
Clearance reflects the ability to eliminate the drug.
Vd can never be greater than total body water.
The half-life of a drug depends on Vd and Cl.

questions.text: Significant drug interaction at albumin binding sites occurs mainly with which of the following characters?
questions.explanation: Extensively protein-bound drugs cause significant displacement interactions because a small displacement produces a large rise in free drug concentration.
questions.keyConcept: Highly protein-bound drugs cause major displacement interactions.
options: Increased body weight of the patient
Drugs with high volume of distribution

questions.text: The following characteristic of a drug tends to reduce its volume of distribution:
questions.explanation: High plasma protein binding keeps drug in the vascular compartment, lowering Vd. Low ionization, high lipid solubility, and high tissue binding all increase Vd.
questions.keyConcept: High plasma protein binding lowers Vd (drug retained in plasma).

questions.text: The following characteristic of a drug tends to reduce its volume of distribution:
questions.explanation: High plasma protein binding keeps drug within the plasma compartment, limiting tissue distribution and lowering Vd. Low ionisation, high lipid solubility and tissue binding all increase Vd.
questions.keyConcept: High plasma protein binding confines drug to plasma, lowering Vd.

questions.text: The following do not affect drug distribution:
questions.explanation: Bioavailability concerns the fraction absorbed into the circulation, not how the drug is subsequently distributed.
questions.keyConcept: Bioavailability affects absorption, not distribution.

questions.text: The following do not affect drug distribution:
questions.explanation: Bioavailability is an absorption parameter and does not influence distribution; perfusion, lipophilicity and protein binding all do.
questions.keyConcept: Bioavailability affects absorption, not distribution.

questions.text: The following drug does not readily cross to the CNS except in meningitis:
questions.explanation: Penicillin poorly penetrates the blood-brain barrier but crosses when the meninges are inflamed in meningitis.
questions.keyConcept: Penicillin crosses the BBB only when meninges are inflamed.

questions.text: The following drugs do not readily cross into the CNS:
questions.explanation: Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier and quaternary neostigmine is poorly lipid-soluble, so neither readily enters the CNS; levodopa and atropine do.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine and neostigmine do not readily cross the BBB.

questions.text: The following drugs do not readily cross to the CNS:
questions.explanation: Dopamine is too polar to cross the blood-brain barrier (hence levodopa, which does cross, is used in parkinsonism), and neostigmine is a quaternary ammonium compound that also cannot cross. Levodopa and atropine (a tertiary amine) do cross.
questions.keyConcept: Highly polar or quaternary drugs (dopamine, neostigmine) do not cross the blood-brain barrier.

questions.text: The following drugs do not readily cross to the CNS in meningitis:
questions.explanation: Even with inflamed meninges, streptomycin and tetracycline penetrate the CNS poorly; rifampicin and penicillins cross adequately when meninges are inflamed.
questions.keyConcept: Streptomycin and tetracycline penetrate inflamed meninges poorly.

questions.text: The following statements are correct except:
questions.explanation: Low extraction-ratio drugs have enzyme-dependent (capacity-limited) clearance, not flow-dependent clearance. They do have high oral bioavailability.
questions.keyConcept: Low extraction-ratio drugs have enzyme-dependent clearance.
options: Bioavailability is the fraction of the drug reaching systemic circulation active after any route of administration.
Shifting the concentration-response curve downward is the character of a non-competitive antagonist.
Clearance is the volume of plasma from which drug is eliminated per unit time.
Drugs with low extraction ratio have high bioavailability and their clearance is flow dependent.

questions.text: The lipophilic part of a drug (non-ionised form) will have reduced:
questions.explanation: The un-ionised lipophilic form is readily reabsorbed from the renal tubules, reducing renal excretion. It actually increases absorption and Vd.
questions.keyConcept: Lipophilic un-ionised drug is reabsorbed renally, lowering excretion.

questions.text: The lipophilic part of a drug will have reduced:
questions.explanation: Lipophilic drugs are passively reabsorbed by renal tubules, so their renal excretion is reduced.
questions.keyConcept: Lipophilicity reduces renal excretion.

questions.text: The loading dose of a drug is governed by its:
questions.explanation: The loading dose is calculated from the volume of distribution (Loading dose = Vd x target Css) to rapidly achieve therapeutic levels.
questions.keyConcept: Loading dose is determined by the volume of distribution.

questions.text: The previous drug X has the following properties EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Because the drug is confined to plasma (small Vd), haemodialysis would in fact be useful; therefore the statement that it is not useful is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: A plasma-confined drug is readily removed by dialysis.
options: Haemodialysis is not useful in treatment of its toxicity.

questions.text: Vd of drug A is 110 L given to a patient whose body weight is 70 kg. Drug A has the following characters:
questions.explanation: A very large Vd (110 L) indicates extensive tissue distribution with low plasma protein binding, making haemodialysis ineffective; none of the listed characters apply.
questions.keyConcept: A large Vd means extensive tissue distribution and ineffective dialysis.
options: Haemodialysis is used in treatment of its toxicity.

questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement?
questions.explanation: L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier (via an amino-acid transporter) whereas dopamine cannot; this is why L-dopa is used in Parkinsonism.
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa crosses the BBB; dopamine does not.
options: Lipid soluble drugs pass freely through the BBB.
Morphine may induce respiratory depression in the foetus if taken during labour.
Dopamine can cross the BBB while L-dopa cannot cross.

questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding lipophilicity:
questions.explanation: Lipophilicity increases hepatic metabolism because the liver processes lipophilic compounds; it also lowers renal excretion and raises Vd and absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Lipophilic drugs are handled by hepatic metabolism, not reduced by it.

questions.text: Which of the following is Wrong?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine concentrates in tissues such as liver, spleen and retina, not primarily the thyroid gland.
questions.keyConcept: Chloroquine accumulates in tissues, not chiefly the thyroid.
options: Vd of a drug may be higher than total body fluid.
Increased Vd of a drug increases its ability to dissolve and distribute in water.
Chloroquine is concentrated in the thyroid gland.
Nitroglycerine has extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism.

questions.text: Which value should also be known to calculate the initial loading dose?
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Css × Vd / F. With Vd known, the target steady-state concentration (Css) is also required.
questions.keyConcept: Loading dose = Css × Vd; requires the target Css.

questions.text: Which value should also be known to calculate the initial loading dose?
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Vd x target Cp, so the target plasma concentration must be known in addition to Vd.
questions.keyConcept: Loading dose needs Vd and target Cp.

questions.text: Administration of drugs may affect the metabolism of other drugs. Discuss this statement.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Enzyme inducers and inhibitors alter metabolism of co-administered drugs.
questions.modelAnswer: Certain drugs induce the microsomal enzyme systems, increasing their activity and the metabolism of other drugs, leading to drug interactions (e.g., rifampicin increases warfarin metabolism). Other drugs inhibit the microsomal enzyme systems, decreasing their activity and reducing the metabolism of other drugs, which can also cause significant interactions.

questions.text: Define enzyme induction, give one example, and mention its clinical significance.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Enzyme induction raises enzyme activity, causing tolerance and drug interactions, and is reversible.
questions.modelAnswer: Enzyme induction is the stimulation of microsomal enzyme systems by certain drugs, increasing their activity. It increases metabolism of the inducing drug (causing tolerance, e.g., phenobarbitone), increases metabolism of other drugs (causing interactions, e.g., rifampicin and warfarin) and increases metabolism of endogenous substrates. Enzyme induction is reversible.

questions.text: Define first-pass metabolism and enumerate two drugs that undergo or reduce hepatic first-pass metabolism.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: First-pass metabolism occurs in liver, gut wall or lungs before systemic circulation.
questions.modelAnswer: First-pass metabolism is the metabolism of some drugs during a single passage through the liver, gut wall or lungs before reaching the systemic circulation. Examples associated with first-pass handling include propranolol and erythromycin.

questions.text: Describe the criteria of a drug to induce serious drug interactions.
questions.explanation: Such drugs experience large changes in free concentration or clearance from small perturbations, making interactions clinically dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Narrow index, high protein binding, and enzyme modulation drive serious interactions.
questions.modelAnswer: Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, those extensively bound to plasma proteins, and potent enzyme inducers or inhibitors are most likely to cause serious interactions.

questions.text: Discuss phenytoin kinetics and its clinical significance.
questions.explanation: Because elimination becomes saturated, small dose increases cause disproportionate rises in plasma concentration and toxicity, requiring careful monitoring.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin shows saturation kinetics and a narrow index, complicating dosing.
questions.modelAnswer: Phenytoin exhibits saturation (zero-order) kinetics with a narrow therapeutic index; it is also an enzyme inducer with variable bioavailability, which leads to drug interactions and makes dosing challenging.

questions.text: Discuss the factors affecting hepatic first-pass metabolism.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Reduced portal flow and hepatic enzyme inhibition lower first-pass metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer: Hepatic first-pass metabolism is reduced by a fall in portal blood flow (e.g., portal hypertension, propranolol) and by inhibition of hepatic enzymes (e.g., liver failure or enzyme inhibitors such as erythromycin).

questions.text: Explain why drug X bioavailability is known to be 60% but on oral administration it was found to be 80%.
questions.explanation: Anything that lowers hepatic metabolism allows more drug to reach the systemic circulation, raising measured bioavailability above the expected value.
questions.keyConcept: Reduced first-pass metabolism raises oral bioavailability.
questions.modelAnswer: The increased oral bioavailability indicates reduced first-pass metabolism, which may be due to liver cirrhosis, decreased portal blood flow, or co-administration of enzyme inhibitors.

questions.text: Explain why prodrugs should be given orally.
questions.explanation: Oral dosing routes the prodrug through hepatic metabolism, which performs the biotransformation needed to generate the active drug.
questions.keyConcept: Oral prodrugs rely on hepatic first-pass metabolism for activation.
questions.modelAnswer: Prodrugs are inactive forms that require metabolic activation, usually in the liver, so oral administration allows them to pass through the liver via first-pass metabolism and be converted to their active form.

questions.text: Explain why propranolol oral dose is 40 mg while its IV dose is 1 mg.
questions.explanation: Oral propranolol is largely metabolised before reaching the circulation, lowering its bioavailability and requiring a higher dose than the IV route, which bypasses first-pass metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Extensive first-pass metabolism makes oral propranolol doses far larger than IV.
questions.modelAnswer: Propranolol undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism after oral dosing, so a much higher oral dose is needed to achieve the same systemic concentration as the intravenous dose.

questions.text: List four factors that may affect drug metabolism.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Age, disease, genetics and enzyme induction/inhibition affect metabolism.
questions.modelAnswer: Factors include physiological changes (age, sex), pathological factors (liver cell failure affecting hepatic activity), pharmacogenetic variations (slow and fast acetylators) and enzyme induction or inhibition.

questions.text: Mention one example of drug categories that may cause drug interactions of clinical significance.
questions.explanation: A small change in concentration of a narrow therapeutic index drug can cause toxicity or loss of effect, making interactions clinically important.
questions.keyConcept: Narrow therapeutic index drugs are prone to serious interactions.
questions.modelAnswer: Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index (e.g. warfarin, digoxin, phenytoin) are a category prone to clinically significant interactions.

questions.text: 1st order kinetic: which of the following is true:
questions.explanation: In first-order kinetics, the rate of elimination is directly proportional to the drug's plasma concentration.
questions.keyConcept: First-order elimination rate is proportional to concentration.
options: A half-life of a drug is proportional to its plasma concentration
The amount eliminated per unit time is constant
The rate of elimination is proportional to drug concentration
Elimination involves a rate limited enzymatic reaction acting maximally

questions.text: A 48-year-old woman on warfarin is prescribed an antibiotic that is a liver microsomal enzyme inducer and may reduce warfarin serum level and action. Which is the prescribed antibiotic?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, accelerating warfarin metabolism and reducing its level and anticoagulant effect.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin induces metabolism and lowers warfarin effect.

questions.text: A main determinant of bioavailability (F) following oral administration is:
questions.explanation: The hepatic extraction ratio is a key determinant of oral bioavailability.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic extraction ratio is the main determinant of oral F.

questions.text: All following are correct regarding a high hepatic extraction ratio drug except:
questions.explanation: High hepatic extraction ratio drugs are flow-limited, making them less susceptible to changes from enzyme induction/inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: High-extraction drugs are flow-limited, not enzyme-sensitive.
options: Liable for enzyme induction and inhibition

questions.text: All of the following is incorrect as regard 1st pass elimination except:
questions.explanation: Per the source answer key the intended answer is D. Note: physiologically the unambiguously true statement is that the liver may excrete drug into bile (option C); first-pass metabolism does not directly reduce Vd, so this item contains a source inconsistency.
questions.keyConcept: First-pass elimination occurs in gut wall and liver and reduces bioavailability.
options: Drug metabolism does not occur in the intestinal wall
Hepatic first pass effect reduces elimination half-life
The liver may excrete the drug into the bile
First pass effect (metabolism) reduces the Vd

questions.text: All the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Clearance is used to calculate the maintenance dose, not the loading dose (which depends on Vd).
questions.keyConcept: Clearance determines maintenance dose; Vd determines loading dose.
options: Elimination t1/2 determines the Tss of the drug
Clearance is used to calculate the loading dose
Loading dose is the dose needed to reach Css
When t = t1/2 it indicates the body contains double its therapeutic dose

questions.text: As regard drug interaction: all of the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Phenobarbitone is an enzyme inducer, so it would increase (not decrease) the metabolism of theophylline.
questions.keyConcept: Phenobarbitone induces enzymes and increases theophylline metabolism.
options: Aspirin displaces warfarin leading to bleeding
Sulphonamides displace bilirubin in neonates causing kernicterus
Antacids decrease the absorption of tetracyclines from gut

questions.text: Conjugation in the body may result in a drug becoming:
questions.explanation: Phase II conjugation adds a polar group, making the drug more water-soluble (more polar) and usually less toxic, favouring excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Conjugation makes drugs more polar and less toxic.

questions.text: Drug A is basic and follows first order kinetics. Its pKa is 9, Vd is 300 L, and clearance is hepatic. Hepatic clearance is defined as:
questions.explanation: Clearance is the volume of blood/plasma completely cleared of drug per unit time, not an amount of drug.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance = volume of blood cleared of drug per unit time.
options: Volume of blood cleared from drug per unit time
Amount of drug removed from circulation per unit time
Amount of drug excreted by the kidney per unit time

questions.text: Drug metabolism in humans usually results in a product that is:
questions.explanation: Drug metabolism typically converts drugs into less lipid-soluble (more water-soluble) products for easier excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Metabolism yields less lipid-soluble, more excretable products.
options: More likely to be reabsorbed by kidney tubules
More lipid soluble than the original drug
Less lipid soluble than the original drug
Less water soluble than the original drug

questions.text: Drug/s reducing hepatic 1st pass metabolism is/are:
questions.explanation: Erythromycin (enzyme inhibitor) and propranolol (reduces hepatic blood flow) both reduce hepatic first-pass metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Enzyme inhibitors and drugs reducing hepatic blood flow lower first-pass metabolism.

questions.text: Drug(s) with saturation kinetics and narrow therapeutic index:
questions.explanation: Phenytoin and theophylline both show saturation (zero-order) kinetics with narrow therapeutic indices.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin and theophylline show saturation kinetics and narrow TI.

questions.text: Drug(s) with saturation kinetics & narrow therapeutic index:
questions.explanation: Phenytoin and theophylline are classic examples of drugs with saturation kinetics and a narrow therapeutic index.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin and theophylline show saturation kinetics with narrow therapeutic index.

questions.text: Drugs reducing hepatic first-pass metabolism:
questions.explanation: Propranolol (saturates first-pass) and erythromycin (enzyme inhibitor) reduce hepatic first-pass metabolism; rifampicin is an enzyme inducer that increases it.
questions.keyConcept: Enzyme inhibition (erythromycin) and saturation (propranolol) reduce first-pass.

questions.text: Enzyme inducers include:
questions.explanation: Phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, and rifampicin are all classic hepatic enzyme inducers.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone, and rifampicin induce enzymes.

questions.text: Enzyme inhibitors include:
questions.explanation: Chloramphenicol, erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, and ketoconazole are all known enzyme inhibitors.
questions.keyConcept: Chloramphenicol, erythromycin, ciprofloxacin and ketoconazole inhibit CYP enzymes.

questions.text: Extraction ratio (E) of a drug is:
questions.explanation: Extraction ratio is the fraction of drug removed from blood during a single pass through the liver.
questions.keyConcept: Extraction ratio = fraction removed per hepatic pass.
options: Fraction of the drug eliminated by the liver
Volume of blood cleared by the liver per unit time
Volume of a fluid cleared from the drug per unit time

questions.text: Extraction ratio is:
questions.explanation: Extraction ratio is the fraction of drug removed from blood during a single pass through the liver.
questions.keyConcept: Extraction ratio = fraction of drug removed in one hepatic pass.
options: Fraction of the drug eliminated by the liver
Volume of blood cleared by the liver per unit time
Volume of fluid cleared from drug per unit time
Amount of the drug eliminated by the liver

questions.text: In first-order kinetics, the following statement/s is/are true except:
questions.explanation: In first-order kinetics, a constant fraction (not a constant amount) of the drug is eliminated per unit time.
questions.keyConcept: First-order: constant fraction eliminated per unit time.
options: Elimination rate is directly proportional to plasma concentration
Constant amount of the drug is eliminated per unit time

questions.text: In which organ is the majority of cytochrome P450 most highly expressed?
questions.explanation: The liver contains the highest concentration of cytochrome P450 enzymes and is the main site of drug metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: The liver has the highest CYP450 expression.

questions.text: In zero-order kinetics, the following is incorrect:
questions.explanation: In zero-order kinetics, a constant amount (not a constant fraction) is eliminated per unit time.
questions.keyConcept: Zero-order: constant amount eliminated per unit time.
options: Half-life (t1/2) of the drug is different at high and low concentration
Steady-state plasma concentration is not achieved
Ethanol is a famous example of a drug with zero-order kinetics
Constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time

questions.text: Microsomal enzymes include:
questions.explanation: Microsomal enzymes include the CYP450 mixed-function oxidases and glucuronyl transferase; dehydrogenases and esterases are non-microsomal.
questions.keyConcept: CYP450 and glucuronyl transferase are microsomal enzymes.

questions.text: Microsomal enzymes include:
questions.explanation: The CYP450 system and glucuronyl transferase are microsomal (endoplasmic reticulum) enzymes; dehydrogenases and esterases are non-microsomal.
questions.keyConcept: CYP450 and glucuronyl transferase are microsomal enzymes.

questions.text: Microsomal enzymes liable for induction include is/are:
questions.explanation: The CYP450 enzyme system and glucuronyl transferase are microsomal enzymes susceptible to induction.
questions.keyConcept: CYP450 and glucuronyl transferase are inducible microsomal enzymes.

questions.text: Regarding pharmacokinetics, choose the incorrect answer:
questions.explanation: Low hepatic extraction ratio drugs are affected by enzyme induction because their clearance is primarily enzyme dependent.
questions.keyConcept: Low-extraction drugs are capacity (enzyme) limited; high-extraction drugs are flow limited.
options: High hepatic extraction ratio (E) drugs are flow dependent
Low hepatic extraction ratio drugs are not affected by enzyme induction
High hepatic extraction ratio drugs have low bioavailability
Cl of high extraction ratio drugs are affected by heart failure

questions.text: The addition of glucuronic acid to a drug:
questions.explanation: Glucuronidation is a Phase II conjugation reaction that increases water solubility and usually inactivates the drug; it is deficient in newborns and does not involve CYP450.
questions.keyConcept: Glucuronidation (Phase II) inactivates drugs and increases water solubility.
options: Usually leads to inactivation of the drug
Is an example of a Phase I reaction
Occurs at the same rate in adults and newborns

questions.text: The addition of glucuronic acid to drug X - choose the correct:
questions.explanation: Glucuronidation is a phase II conjugation that increases water solubility and usually inactivates the drug; it does not involve CYP450.
questions.keyConcept: Glucuronidation usually inactivates and solubilises drugs.
options: Usually leads to inactivation of the drug
Is an example of a phase I reaction

questions.text: The following conditions or drugs can increase oral bioavailability of a lipophilic drug except:
questions.explanation: Phenytoin is an enzyme inducer, which decreases bioavailability by increasing metabolism, not increasing it.
questions.keyConcept: Enzyme inducers lower oral bioavailability of lipophilic drugs.

questions.text: The following does not decrease the hepatic first pass metabolism:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer, which would increase first-pass metabolism, not decrease it.
questions.keyConcept: Enzyme inducers increase first-pass metabolism.

questions.text: The following has increased rate of drug metabolism:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is a known enzyme inducer, increasing the rate of drug metabolism.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin induces enzymes and increases metabolism.

questions.text: The following is a phase II reaction:
questions.explanation: Acetylation is a Phase II conjugation reaction; reduction, hydrolysis, and oxidation are Phase I reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Acetylation is a Phase II conjugation reaction.

questions.text: The following is/are a phase 2 reaction/s of drug metabolism:
questions.explanation: Conjugation is the primary type of Phase II drug metabolism reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Conjugation is the hallmark Phase II reaction.

questions.text: The following is/are a phase II reaction(s):
questions.explanation: Acetylation is a phase II conjugation reaction; reduction, hydrolysis and oxidation are phase I reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Acetylation is a phase II conjugation reaction.

questions.text: The following is/are a phase II reaction(s) of drug metabolism:
questions.explanation: Conjugation is the defining phase II reaction; reduction, hydrolysis and oxidation are phase I.
questions.keyConcept: Conjugation is the phase II reaction.

questions.text: The following is not true concerning factors affecting drug clearance:
questions.explanation: Clearance is DIRECTLY proportional to organ blood flow (A wrong) and is independent of Vd (D wrong); hence A and D are the untrue statements.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance is proportional to organ blood flow and independent of Vd.
options: It is inversely proportional to the blood flow to the clearing organ
It is inversely proportional to binding of the drug to plasma proteins
It is directly proportional to the activity of secretary processes
It is directly proportional to volume of distribution

questions.text: The following is not true concerning factors affecting drug clearance:
questions.explanation: Clearance is DIRECTLY (not inversely) proportional to organ blood flow; A is the untrue statement.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance increases with organ blood flow.
options: It is inversely proportional to the blood flow to the clearing organ
It is inversely proportional to binding of the drug to plasma proteins
It is directly proportional to the activity of secretory processes

questions.text: The following is wrong concerning biotransformation phase 1 reactions:

questions.keyConcept: Phase I reactions unmask/introduce polar groups rather than forming conjugates.
options: Include oxidation by CYP450 enzyme system
Convert drug to an easily excreted ionised metabolite
Result in formation of non-toxic polar conjugates
Some drugs may still be active

questions.text: The following is WRONG concerning biotransformation phase I reactions:

questions.keyConcept: Conjugate formation is Phase II, not Phase I.
options: Include oxidation by CYP450, reduction and hydrolysis
Convert drug to an easily excreted ionized metabolite
