questions.text: The following is wrong concerning biotransformation phase I reactions:
questions.explanation: Formation of conjugates is a phase II reaction, not phase I, so this statement is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Conjugate formation is phase II, not phase I.
options: Include oxidation by the CYP450 enzyme system
Convert the drug to an easily excreted ionized metabolite
Result in formation of nontoxic polar conjugates
Some drugs may still be active

questions.text: The following is wrong concerning biotransformation phase I reactions:
questions.explanation: Conjugate formation belongs to phase II, so describing it as a phase I outcome is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Conjugates are products of phase II, not phase I.
options: Include oxidation by the CYP450 enzyme system, reduction and hydrolysis
Convert the drug to an easily excreted ionized metabolite
Result in formation of non-toxic polar, rapidly eliminated conjugates

questions.text: The Vd of drug X is 110 L and it is given to a patient whose body weight is 70 kg. Drug X has the following character(s):
questions.explanation: A Vd of 110 L (greater than total body water) indicates extensive tissue distribution, low plasma protein binding, and unsuitability for haemodialysis, so none of the listed characters apply.
questions.keyConcept: A large Vd implies extensive tissue distribution and poor dialysability.
options: Haemodialysis is used in treatment of its toxicity

questions.text: When drug/drug interactions involve inhibition of metabolism, which of the following types of drugs are of the most concern?
questions.explanation: Inhibition of metabolism for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index is critical due to the high toxicity risk with slight concentration increases.
questions.keyConcept: Enzyme inhibition is most dangerous for narrow-therapeutic-index drugs.
options: Drugs that are highly bound to albumin
Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index
Drugs with a high extraction ratio
Short acting drugs that are used in single doses

questions.text: When the extraction ratio (E) of a drug is more than 0.6 its clearance is:
questions.explanation: A high extraction ratio (E > 0.6) makes hepatic clearance limited by, and proportional to, hepatic blood flow (flow-dependent / perfusion-limited).
questions.keyConcept: High extraction ratio (>0.6) gives flow-dependent clearance.

questions.text: Which of the following best explains the critical event that leads to liver failure following acetaminophen toxicity?
questions.explanation: Acetaminophen overdose generates the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which depletes hepatic glutathione; the unconjugated NAPQI then binds hepatocytes and causes necrosis.
questions.keyConcept: Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity results from glutathione depletion (NAPQI).

questions.text: Which of the following definition(s) is/are incorrect?
questions.explanation: Clearance is a VOLUME cleared per unit time, not an amount; A is the incorrect definition. B and C are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance is a volume (not an amount) cleared per unit time.
options: Systemic clearance is the amount of drug cleared from circulation per unit time
Extraction ratio is the fraction of the drug eliminated by the liver
Hepatic clearance is the volume of blood cleared by the liver per unit time

questions.text: Which of the following definition(s) is (are) incorrect:
questions.explanation: Systemic clearance is the volume of fluid cleared of drug per unit time, not the amount.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance is a volume cleared per unit time, not an amount.
options: Extraction ratio: fraction of the drug eliminated by the liver
Systemic clearance: amount of drug cleared from circulation per unit time
Hepatic clearance: volume of blood cleared by the liver per unit time
Plasma half-life is directly proportional to volume of distribution

questions.text: Which of the following drugs is/are wrongly matched to the site of first-pass metabolism?
questions.explanation: Per the source key, the estrogen and nitroglycerin pairings are considered the wrongly matched ones — nitroglycerin undergoes hepatic/vascular (not purely intestinal) first-pass metabolism. Propranolol/hepatic and nicotine pairings are accepted.
questions.keyConcept: Nitroglycerin first-pass metabolism is hepatic/vascular, not intestinal.

questions.text: Which of the following is a true statement?
questions.explanation: Theophylline shows saturation (zero-order at high dose) kinetics and a narrow therapeutic index. Acetylation is Phase II; first-order eliminates a constant fraction (not amount); zero-order drugs have no fixed t½; the SL route bypasses first-pass.
questions.keyConcept: Theophylline has saturation kinetics and a narrow therapeutic index.
options: Acetylation is a phase I reaction
Theophylline is a drug with saturation kinetics and a narrow therapeutic index
A constant amount of a drug with first order kinetics is eliminated per unit time
Css of drugs with zero-order kinetics is achieved after 4-5 t½
The first pass effect is most likely to occur if the drug is given sublingually

questions.text: Which of the following is a true statement?
questions.explanation: Theophylline characteristically exhibits saturation kinetics and has a narrow therapeutic index.
questions.keyConcept: Theophylline shows saturation (zero-order) kinetics with a narrow therapeutic index.
options: Acetylation is a phase I reaction
A constant amount of a drug with 1st order kinetics is eliminated per unit time
Steady-state plasma concentration of drugs with zero-order is achieved after 4 t1/2
The first-pass effect is most likely to occur if the drug is given sublingually
Theophylline is a drug with saturation kinetics and narrow therapeutic index

questions.text: Which of the following is a true statement concerning drug clearance?
questions.explanation: When the extraction ratio E < 0.2, hepatic clearance is capacity/enzyme-limited. Clearance is used for maintenance (not loading) dose, is directly proportional to organ blood flow, and lipid solubility decreases renal excretion.
questions.keyConcept: Low extraction ratio (E < 0.2) gives enzyme-dependent (capacity-limited) clearance.
options: Clearance is useful in calculation of the loading dose
When E is less than 0.2, its clearance is nearly enzyme dependent
It is inversely proportional to the blood flow to the clearing organ
Lipid solubility increases renal excretion of drugs
It is directly proportional to volume of distribution

questions.text: Which of the following is not an enzyme inducer?
questions.explanation: Erythromycin is a hepatic enzyme inhibitor; the others are classic inducers.
questions.keyConcept: Erythromycin is an enzyme inhibitor, not an inducer.

questions.text: Which of the following is not an enzyme inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer; the others are inhibitors.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer, not an inhibitor.

questions.text: Which of the following is/or are microsomal enzyme?
questions.explanation: Glucuronyl transferase and cytochrome oxidase are classified as microsomal enzymes.
questions.keyConcept: Glucuronyl transferase and CYP oxidases are microsomal enzymes.

questions.text: Changes in doses cannot be tolerated with ethanol. Explain.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Ethanol's zero-order elimination makes small dose changes dangerous.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethanol is eliminated by zero-order kinetics, so even modest changes in dose can cause a disproportionate rise in concentration and toxicity.

questions.text: Compare between first-order and zero-order kinetic drugs in terms of elimination and amount of drug eliminated per unit time.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: First-order eliminates a constant fraction; zero-order eliminates a constant amount.
questions.modelAnswer: In first-order kinetics, elimination is proportional to the plasma concentration and a constant fraction (percentage) of the drug is eliminated per unit time. In zero-order kinetics, elimination is constant and a constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time.

questions.text: Compare between first-order and zero-order kinetic drugs in terms of metabolizing enzymes, steady-state concentration and half-life.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: First-order: constant t1/2 and true steady state; zero-order: saturable enzymes with overshooting levels.
questions.modelAnswer: First-order drugs have unlimited (unsaturated) metabolizing enzymes, a constant half-life and reach a steady-state concentration on repeated dosing (steady state in 4-5 half-lives). Zero-order drugs have limited (saturated) metabolizing enzymes, a variable half-life and do not reach a true steady state on repeated dosing, so the concentration overshoots and increasing the dose disproportionately raises the concentration.

questions.text: Define saturation kinetics.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Saturation kinetics is the shift from first-order to zero-order once elimination is saturated.
questions.modelAnswer: A drug follows first-order kinetics at small doses but switches to zero-order kinetics at high doses when the elimination mechanism becomes saturated; this dose-dependent change is termed saturation kinetics.

questions.text: Define systemic drug clearance.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Systemic clearance = rate of elimination/concentration = sum of organ clearances.
questions.modelAnswer: Systemic clearance is the volume of fluid cleared of the drug per unit time: CL = rate of elimination / drug concentration. It equals the sum of the individual organ clearances (liver, kidney, lung, etc.), so total clearance = renal clearance + non-renal clearance.

questions.text: Define the elimination half-life of a drug.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.modelAnswer: The elimination half-life is the time required to reduce the plasma concentration of a drug to half of its initial concentration: t1/2 = 0.693 x Vd / CL.

questions.text: Discuss the factors affecting drug clearance and their relation to clearance.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance rises with organ blood flow and removal activity, and falls with protein binding.
questions.modelAnswer: Clearance is directly proportional to blood flow to the clearing organ, inversely proportional to binding of the drug to plasma proteins, and directly proportional to the activity of the processes responsible for drug removal such as hepatic enzymes, glomerular filtration rate and secretory processes.

questions.text: Discuss the significance of determining drug clearance.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance sets the maintenance dose (CL x Css) and guides renal dose adjustment.
questions.modelAnswer: Clearance is used to calculate the maintenance dose (MD = CL x Css). For drugs eliminated by glomerular filtration, the dosing regimen can be guided by creatinine clearance, for example the dosing of gentamicin.

questions.text: Enumerate the effect of kidney function on the dose of gentamicin.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Gentamicin dose is reduced in proportion to falling creatinine clearance.
questions.modelAnswer: With normal kidney function (creatinine clearance about 120 ml/min) give 80 mg three times daily; at a creatinine clearance of 60 ml/min give half the usual dose; and at a creatinine clearance of 30 ml/min give one quarter the usual dose.

questions.text: Enumerate the factors affecting renal elimination and how they affect drug excretion.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: GFR, protein binding and lipophilicity/urine pH govern renal excretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Renal elimination is affected by the glomerular filtration rate, by plasma protein binding (which prevents filtration of bound drug), and by drug lipophilicity (influenced by urine pH and drug pKa), which enhances tubular reabsorption of the filtered drug.

questions.text: Mention one example of a drug category that may cause drug interactions of clinical significance.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Drugs with steep dose-response curves cause significant interactions.
questions.modelAnswer: Drugs with a steep (narrow) dose-response curve are prone to clinically significant drug interactions.

questions.text: Mention the factors affecting the elimination half-life.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Organ function, drug delivery, protein binding and Vd affect half-life.
questions.modelAnswer: The half-life depends on the state of the eliminating organs (liver and kidney function) and on the delivery of the drug to those organs. Plasma protein binding limits renal filtration, and drugs with a very high volume of distribution may escape elimination by being held in the tissues.

questions.text: Mention the significance of saturation kinetics.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Saturation kinetics causes unpredictable toxicity and frequent interactions.
questions.modelAnswer: With saturation kinetics, modest changes in dose or bioavailability can cause unexpected toxicity, and drug interactions are more common (e.g., phenytoin and theophylline).

questions.text: Mention two clinical values of the elimination half-life.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Half-life guides dosing interval and time to steady state (4-5 t1/2).
questions.modelAnswer: The half-life determines the dosage interval (T): if T equals t1/2 the body stores about twice the dose (accepted for most drugs), if T is shorter than t1/2 more accumulation occurs, and if T is longer than t1/2 the concentration falls between doses. It also indicates the time to reach steady state (about 4-5 half-lives).

questions.text: What factors might contribute to the elimination of a drug from the blood?
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Drugs leave the blood by metabolism and excretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Metabolism and excretion contribute to the elimination of a drug from the blood.

questions.text: Match the pharmacokinetic parameter or term to the appropriate statement.
questions.explanation: Hepatic extraction determines oral bioavailability; Vd equals dose divided by initial plasma concentration; bioequivalent drugs share identical AUCs; and systemic clearance equals elimination rate divided by drug concentration.
questions.keyConcept: Each pharmacokinetic parameter has a distinct defining relationship.

pairs.premise: A main determinant of bioavailability (F) following oral administration.
pairs.target: Hepatic extraction

pairs.premise: Can be calculated for drugs administered IV by dividing the bolus dose by the initial resultant plasma concentration.
pairs.target: Volume of distribution (Vd)

pairs.premise: Used to describe drugs with identical areas under the curve (AUCs).
pairs.target: Bioequivalence

pairs.premise: Can be calculated by dividing rate of elimination by drug concentration.
pairs.target: Systemic clearance (CLs)

questions.text: Alkalization of urine by giving bicarbonate is used to treat phenobarbital (weak acid) overdose. Which best describes the rationale for alkalization of urine in this setting?
questions.explanation: Alkaline urine ionizes the weak acid phenobarbital, trapping it in the tubular lumen and reducing its reabsorption, which enhances its excretion (ion trapping).
questions.keyConcept: Alkaline urine ionizes and traps weak acids, reducing reabsorption.
options: To reduce tubular reabsorption of phenobarbital
To increase glomerular filtration of phenobarbital
To increase tubular reabsorption of phenobarbital

questions.text: All of the following are correct regarding a high hepatic extraction ratio drug except:
questions.explanation: High-extraction drugs have flow-dependent clearance, so they are relatively unaffected by enzyme induction/inhibition; that susceptibility belongs to low-extraction drugs.
questions.keyConcept: High-extraction drugs are flow-limited, not enzyme-sensitive.
options: Liable for enzyme induction and inhibition

questions.text: Characteristics of first-order kinetics include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Steady state is reached after about 4-5 half-lives, not 3-4, so this statement is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Steady state needs ~4-5 half-lives.
options: The rate of elimination is proportional to drug concentration
Most first-order drugs are safer than saturation-kinetics drugs
Steady state is reached after 3-4 half-lives

questions.text: Choose the correct answer:
questions.explanation: Total systemic clearance equals the sum of all organ clearances (e.g. hepatic + renal); weak bases are poorly absorbed in the acidic stomach and high-Vd drugs resist dialysis.
questions.keyConcept: Systemic clearance = sum of organ clearances.
options: Weak bases are absorbed efficiently across the gastric mucosa
Co-administration of atropine speeds absorption of all drugs
Drugs with large Vd can be removed effectively by hemodialysis
Systemic clearance is the sum of individual organ clearances

questions.text: Clearance is useful in calculation of:
questions.explanation: Clearance is used to calculate the maintenance dose and, with Vd, the plasma half-life (t½ = 0.693 · Vd / CL).
questions.keyConcept: Clearance determines maintenance dose and half-life.

questions.text: Clearance is useful in calculation of:
questions.explanation: Clearance is used to calculate both the maintenance dose and the elimination half-life. The loading dose depends on Vd, not clearance.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance determines maintenance dose and half-life.

questions.text: Clearance is useful in the calculation of:
questions.explanation: Clearance determines the maintenance dose and, together with Vd, the elimination half-life; the loading dose depends on Vd.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance sets maintenance dose and (with Vd) half-life.

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to its potential drug interaction - Aspirin:
questions.explanation: Aspirin displaces warfarin from plasma proteins, raising free warfarin and the risk of bleeding.
questions.keyConcept: Aspirin displaces warfarin, increasing bleeding risk.
options: Theophylline toxicity due to inhibition of its metabolism
Bleeding with warfarin due to displacement from plasma proteins
Risk of pregnancy due to increased metabolism of oral contraceptives
Chelation of Ca2+ and Al3+ in antacids
Kernicterus in the newborn due to displacement of bilirubin from plasma proteins

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to its potential drug interaction - Erythromycin:
questions.explanation: Erythromycin inhibits hepatic enzymes, reducing theophylline metabolism and causing theophylline toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Erythromycin inhibition causes theophylline toxicity.
options: Theophylline toxicity due to inhibition of its metabolism
Bleeding with warfarin due to displacement from plasma proteins
Risk of pregnancy due to increased metabolism of oral contraceptives
Chelation of Ca2+ and Al3+ in antacids
Kernicterus in the newborn due to displacement of bilirubin from plasma proteins

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to its potential drug interaction - Rifampicin:
questions.explanation: Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes, accelerating metabolism of oral contraceptives and risking contraceptive failure.
questions.keyConcept: Rifampicin induction can cause contraceptive failure.
options: Theophylline toxicity due to inhibition of its metabolism
Bleeding with warfarin due to displacement from plasma proteins
Risk of pregnancy due to increased metabolism of oral contraceptives
Chelation of Ca2+ and Al3+ in antacids
Kernicterus in the newborn due to displacement of bilirubin from plasma proteins

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to its potential drug interaction - Sulfonamides:
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides displace bilirubin from plasma proteins in neonates, risking kernicterus.
questions.keyConcept: Sulfonamides displace bilirubin, risking kernicterus.
options: Theophylline toxicity due to inhibition of its metabolism
Bleeding with warfarin due to displacement from plasma proteins
Risk of pregnancy due to increased metabolism of oral contraceptives
Chelation of Ca2+ and Al3+ in antacids
Kernicterus in the newborn due to displacement of bilirubin from plasma proteins

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to its potential drug interaction - Tetracyclines:
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines chelate divalent and trivalent cations (Ca2+, Al3+) in antacids, reducing their absorption.
questions.keyConcept: Tetracyclines chelate cations in antacids.
options: Theophylline toxicity due to inhibition of its metabolism
Bleeding with warfarin due to displacement from plasma proteins
Risk of pregnancy due to increased metabolism of oral contraceptives
Chelation of Ca2+ and Al3+ in antacids
Kernicterus in the newborn due to displacement of bilirubin from plasma proteins

questions.text: Drug A (acidic, pKa 3, t½ 6 hours) most probably:
questions.explanation: A defined, constant half-life (6 h) indicates first-order elimination. As a weak acid (pKa 3) it is better absorbed in an acidic medium where it is non-ionized, not alkaline.
questions.keyConcept: A fixed half-life implies first-order elimination kinetics.
options: Reaches half of its concentration in blood after 24-30 hours
Is well absorbed in alkaline medium

questions.text: Drug X has Vd = 100 L, t1/2 = 4 days, clearance = 4 L/h, and a loading dose of 400 mg. The steady-state concentration is:
questions.explanation: Concentration = dose / Vd = 400 mg / 100 L = 4 mg/L = 4 microgram/ml.
questions.keyConcept: Concentration = dose / Vd.

questions.text: Drug X has Vd = 60 L, t1/2 = 4 days, and CL = 4 L/h. The loading dose to reach a steady-state concentration of 10 mg/L is:
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Vd x target concentration = 60 L x 10 mg/L = 600 mg.
questions.keyConcept: Loading dose = Vd x target plasma concentration.

questions.text: Drugs binding to plasma protein have the following features except:
questions.explanation: Protein binding prolongs (does not shorten) the elimination half-life by reducing the amount of free drug available for elimination.
questions.keyConcept: Plasma protein binding prolongs elimination half-life.
options: Binding facilitates drug absorption by decreasing its free concentration.
Binding limits tissue penetration and decreases Vd.
Binding decreases the free part, which is ineffective in treatment of dangerous infection.

questions.text: Drugs with saturation kinetics and a narrow therapeutic index:
questions.explanation: Phenytoin and theophylline classically show saturation (zero-order) kinetics with a narrow therapeutic index.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin and theophylline show saturation kinetics.

questions.text: Extraction ratio (E) of a drug is:
questions.explanation: Extraction ratio is the fraction of drug removed from the blood as it passes through the liver.
questions.keyConcept: Extraction ratio = fraction removed in one hepatic pass.
options: Volume of blood cleared by the liver per unit time
Volume of fluid cleared of the drug per unit time
Fraction of the drug eliminated by the liver
Amount of the drug eliminated by the liver

questions.text: Hepatic clearance is defined as:
questions.explanation: Hepatic clearance is the volume of blood the liver clears of drug per unit time.
questions.keyConcept: Hepatic clearance is a volume of blood cleared per time.
options: Volume of blood cleared of drug per unit time
Amount of drug removed from circulation per unit time
Amount of drug excreted by the kidney per unit time

questions.text: In first-order kinetics, the following is WRONG:
questions.explanation: At high plasma concentrations theophylline shows ZERO-order (saturation) kinetics, not first-order; the other statements correctly describe first-order kinetics.
questions.keyConcept: High-concentration theophylline follows zero-order, not first-order, kinetics.
options: They generally apply to high plasma concentration of theophylline
The rate of clearance is proportional to concentration
They are more common than zero order kinetics
They result in steady state concentration after multiple dosing

questions.text: In first-order kinetics, the following statement(s) is/are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: In first-order kinetics a constant FRACTION (not amount) is eliminated per unit time; eliminating a constant amount describes zero-order kinetics.
questions.keyConcept: First-order eliminates a constant fraction; zero-order a constant amount.
options: Constant amount of the drug is eliminated per unit time
Elimination rate is directly proportional to plasma concentration

questions.text: In first-order kinetics, the following statement(s) is/are true except:
questions.explanation: First-order kinetics eliminates a constant fraction per unit time; a constant amount is eliminated in zero-order kinetics, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: First-order eliminates a constant fraction, not amount.
options: Elimination rate is directly proportional to plasma concentration
There is a steady-state plasma concentration
A constant amount of the drug is eliminated per unit time

questions.text: In zero-order kinetics, the following is Incorrect:
questions.explanation: Zero-order kinetics eliminates a constant AMOUNT (not fraction) per unit time; eliminating a constant fraction describes first-order kinetics.
questions.keyConcept: Zero-order eliminates a constant amount per unit time.
options: Half-life (t½) of the drug is different at high and low concentration
Constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time
Steady-state plasma concentration is not achieved
Ethanol is a famous example of a drug with zero-order kinetics

questions.text: Regarding drug interactions, all of the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Phenobarbitone is an enzyme inducer and increases (not decreases) theophylline metabolism, so this statement is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Phenobarbitone induces and increases theophylline metabolism.
options: Aspirin displaces warfarin leading to bleeding
Sulfonamides displace bilirubin in neonates causing kernicterus
Antacids decrease the absorption of tetracyclines from the gut

questions.text: Regarding drug pharmacokinetics, the following are correct except:
questions.explanation: Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared per unit time, not the dose/amount eliminated, so this statement is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance is a volume, not an amount, per time.
options: Bioavailability is the fraction of unchanged drug that reaches systemic circulation
Half-life is the time required to reduce plasma concentration to half
Drug clearance is the dose of drug eliminated per unit time
First-pass metabolism is destruction of drug in gut or liver before reaching circulation

questions.text: Regarding drug pharmacokinetics, the following are correct except:
questions.explanation: Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time, not the dose eliminated per unit time.
questions.keyConcept: Clearance is a volume cleared per unit time, not a dose.
options: Bioavailability is the fraction of unchanged drug that reaches systemic circulation.
T1/2 is time required to reduce plasma concentration of drug to its half.
Drug clearance is the dose of the drug eliminated per unit time.
First-pass metabolism is the destruction of drug in gut or liver before reaching systemic circulation.

questions.text: Regarding first-order kinetics, the following is wrong:
questions.explanation: At high plasma concentrations theophylline follows zero-order (saturation) kinetics, not first-order, so this statement is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Theophylline becomes zero-order at high concentrations.
options: The rate of clearance is proportional to concentration
Generally applies to high plasma concentrations of theophylline
Steady-state concentration is reached after multiple dosing

questions.text: Regarding first-order kinetics, which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: First-order kinetics eliminates a constant fraction of drug per unit time and has a fixed half-life.
questions.keyConcept: First-order eliminates a constant fraction per time.
options: A constant amount of drug is eliminated per unit time regardless of concentration
A constant fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time
It is less common than zero-order kinetics
Steady-state concentration is not reached after multiple dosing
Its plasma half-life increases with higher doses

questions.text: Regarding pharmacokinetics, choose the incorrect answer:
questions.explanation: Low-extraction drugs are enzyme-dependent and therefore strongly affected by enzyme induction, so this statement is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Low-extraction drugs are affected by enzyme induction.
options: High hepatic extraction ratio drugs are flow dependent
Low hepatic extraction ratio drugs are not affected by enzyme induction
High hepatic extraction ratio drugs have low bioavailability
Clearance of high extraction ratio drugs is affected by heart failure

questions.text: Significant drug interaction at albumin binding sites occurs mainly with which of the following characters?
questions.explanation: Displacement interactions matter for drugs that are extensively (highly) bound to plasma proteins, because a small displacement greatly raises the free fraction.
questions.keyConcept: Highly protein-bound drugs are prone to displacement interactions.
options: Increased body weight of the patient

questions.text: The following is an incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Saturation-kinetic drugs follow zero-order kinetics at higher doses (enzymes are saturated), not first-order, so this statement is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Saturation kinetics become zero-order at high doses.
options: Apnea may occur with succinylcholine in a patient with pseudocholinesterase deficiency
Rigidity and hyperthermia is an idiosyncratic adverse effect of succinylcholine
Saturation-kinetic drugs obey first-order kinetics at higher doses
Sudden withdrawal of beta-blockers may precipitate angina pectoris

questions.text: The following is an incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Saturation (capacity-limited) kinetic drugs follow zero-order kinetics at higher doses and first-order kinetics only at lower doses.
questions.keyConcept: Saturation kinetics become zero-order at higher doses.
options: Apnoea may occur with succinylcholine in a patient deficient in pseudocholinesterase.
Rigidity and hyperthermia is an idiosyncratic adverse effect of succinylcholine.
Saturation kinetic drugs obey 1st order kinetics at higher doses.
Sudden withdrawal of beta blockers may precipitate angina pectoris.

questions.text: The following is not true concerning factors affecting drug clearance:

questions.keyConcept: Clearance rises with blood flow and is independent of Vd.

Inversely proportional to binding of the drug to plasma proteins

options: It is better absorbed in stomach

questions.keyConcept: Clearance increases with metabolising enzyme activity.
options: Is inversely proportional to blood flow to the clearing organ.
Is directly proportional to binding of drug to plasma proteins.

Is directly proportional to activity of metabolising enzymes.

questions.text: The maintenance dose of Drug A cannot be calculated since the following parameter is missing:
questions.explanation: Maintenance dose is calculated from clearance (rate of dosing = Css × CL). Clearance is the missing value; Vd is used for the loading dose, not the maintenance dose.
questions.keyConcept: Maintenance dose depends on clearance (CL).

questions.text: The maintenance dose of the previous drug if F = 50% is:
questions.explanation: Maintenance dose rate = clearance x target steady-state concentration = 4 L/h x 10 mg/L = 40 mg/h.
questions.keyConcept: Maintenance dose rate = clearance x target concentration.

questions.text: The time needed to reach steady-state concentration of drug A (t1/2 = 6 h) in first-order kinetics is:
questions.explanation: Steady state needs about 4-5 half-lives: 4 x 6 = 24 h to 5 x 6 = 30 h.
questions.keyConcept: Steady state in ~4-5 half-lives.

questions.text: To prolong the duration of drug action all the following are correct except:

questions.text: When the extraction ratio (E) of a drug is 0.6, its clearance is:
questions.explanation: An intermediate extraction ratio (around 0.3-0.7) means clearance depends on both hepatic blood flow and enzyme activity.
questions.keyConcept: Intermediate E gives mixed flow/enzyme-dependent clearance.

questions.text: Which of the following characters does not increase the risk of drug-drug interaction?
questions.explanation: High-extraction (flow-limited) drugs are little affected by enzyme inducers/inhibitors, so they do not raise interaction risk; the others do.
questions.keyConcept: High extraction ratio limits metabolic interaction risk.

questions.text: Which of the following definitions is incorrect?

options: Loading dose = steady-state concentration x CL

questions.text: Which of the following is a true statement concerning drug clearance?

options: Clearance is useful in calculation of the loading dose

questions.explanation: A low extraction ratio (<0.2) means clearance is capacity-limited, i.e. enzyme dependent. Clearance calculates the maintenance dose, increases with blood flow, and lipophilicity reduces renal excretion.

options: Clearance is useful in calculation of loading dose.

subjects.name: Pharmacology
subjects.lectures: Mechanisms of Drugs, Signaling Mechanisms, Dose Response Relationship, Adverse Drug Interactions, Drug Interactions

questions.text: A patient is experiencing a severe anaphylactic reaction to an antibiotic. Which is the best drug to use and why?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline physiologically opposes the effects of anaphylactic mediators.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline is the lifesaving physiological antagonist in anaphylaxis.
questions.modelAnswer: Epinephrine (adrenaline) is the best drug; it reverses bronchospasm and hypotension and is lifesaving in anaphylaxis. It acts as a physiological antagonist to the mediators of anaphylaxis (bronchodilation via beta2, vasoconstriction via alpha1, cardiac stimulation via beta1).

questions.text: Compare between agonist and antagonist as regards affinity and efficacy.
questions.explanation: Both bind, but only the agonist activates the receptor.
questions.keyConcept: Agonists have affinity and efficacy; antagonists have affinity only.
questions.modelAnswer: Affinity: both agonists and antagonists possess affinity (they bind to the receptor). Efficacy: an agonist possesses efficacy (it activates the receptor to produce a response), whereas an antagonist lacks efficacy (it binds but does not activate the receptor).

questions.text: Compare between agonist and antagonist with respect to affinity and efficacy.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Agonists have affinity and efficacy; antagonists have affinity only.
questions.modelAnswer: An agonist binds to the receptor and activates it, possessing both affinity and efficacy. An antagonist binds to the receptor without activating it, possessing affinity but no efficacy.

questions.text: Compare between chemical and physiological non-receptor antagonism in terms of characteristics, with examples.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Chemical antagonism acts away from the receptor; physiological antagonism uses a different receptor.
questions.modelAnswer: Chemical antagonism is a direct interaction between an agonist and an antagonist away from the receptor (e.g., heparin, which carries a negative charge, is neutralized by the positively charged protamine sulfate, its antidote). Physiological antagonism is when one drug antagonizes the effect of another by acting on a different receptor to produce the opposite action (e.g., histamine causes bronchospasm and vasodilation, while epinephrine acts on adrenergic receptors to cause bronchodilation and vasoconstriction).

questions.text: Compare between competitive and non-competitive antagonists in terms of binding of antagonist and duration dependence.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Competitive duration depends on relative drug concentrations; non-competitive depends on receptor turnover.
questions.modelAnswer: A competitive antagonist binds reversibly, competing with the agonist for the same recognition site, and the duration of antagonism depends on the relative plasma concentrations of agonist and antagonist. A non-competitive antagonist binds irreversibly to the recognition site or to an allosteric site, and the duration of antagonism depends on the rate of receptor turnover.

questions.text: Compare between competitive and non-competitive receptor antagonism in terms of characteristics, with examples.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Competitive antagonists share the agonist site reversibly; non-competitive antagonists bind irreversibly or allosterically.
questions.modelAnswer: A competitive antagonist competes with the agonist for the same recognition site of the receptor (e.g., curare antagonizing acetylcholine at the Nm receptor). A non-competitive antagonist binds irreversibly to the same recognition site or binds to an allosteric site (e.g., phenoxybenzamine antagonizing norepinephrine at the alpha receptor).

questions.text: Compare between full agonist and partial agonist.
questions.explanation: A partial agonist gives less than maximal response and can blunt a full agonist.
questions.keyConcept: Partial agonists have lower efficacy and can antagonise full agonists.
questions.modelAnswer: Efficacy: a full agonist produces the maximal possible effect (full efficacy), while a partial agonist produces a sub-maximal effect (lower efficacy). Action alone: a full agonist activates the receptor to its full effect, while a partial agonist activates the receptor but with lower efficacy. Action in presence of a full agonist: a full agonist potentiates the effect, whereas a partial agonist can act as an antagonist by competing with the full agonist and reducing its effect.

questions.text: Compare between up-regulation and down-regulation of receptors.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Antagonists up-regulate, agonists down-regulate receptors.
questions.modelAnswer: Up-regulation is an increase in the number of receptors due to continuous use of an antagonist. Down-regulation is a decrease in the number of receptors due to continuous use of an agonist.

questions.text: Define drug tolerance.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Tolerance = needing higher doses for the same effect after repeated use.
questions.modelAnswer: Drug tolerance is a reduced responsiveness to a drug on repeated administration, so that higher doses are needed to produce the same effect.

questions.text: Discuss types of pharmacological antagonism with examples.
questions.explanation: Antagonism is classified by where and how the antagonist opposes the agonist.
questions.keyConcept: Antagonism may be competitive, non-competitive, chemical or physiological.
questions.modelAnswer: Competitive antagonism: the antagonist competes with the agonist for the same receptor binding site and can be overcome by increasing agonist concentration (e.g. prazosin, an alpha1 antagonist, against noradrenaline). Non-competitive antagonism: the antagonist binds irreversibly or to an allosteric site, reducing the maximal effect and not overcome by raising agonist concentration (e.g. phenoxybenzamine). Chemical antagonism: the antagonist reacts directly with the agonist to inactivate it (e.g. protamine neutralising heparin). Physiological (functional) antagonism: two drugs act on different receptors to produce opposite effects (e.g. epinephrine causing bronchodilation via beta2 counteracting histamine bronchoconstriction via H1 in anaphylaxis).

questions.text: Enumerate 4 differences between competitive and non-competitive antagonists with examples.
questions.explanation: The two differ in binding, reversibility and effect on Emax and ED50.
questions.keyConcept: Competitive antagonists shift ED50 right; non-competitive lower Emax.
questions.modelAnswer: Binding site: competitive antagonists bind the same recognition site as the agonist, while non-competitive antagonists bind an allosteric site or irreversibly to the recognition site. Reversibility: competitive is reversible (overcome by increasing agonist dose), while non-competitive is irreversible or very slowly reversible. Emax (efficacy): unchanged with competitive (agonist can still reach maximum), but decreased with non-competitive. ED50 (potency): increased with competitive (rightward shift of the curve), while with non-competitive the ED50 is less relevant because Emax is reduced. Examples: atropine vs acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors (competitive); phenoxybenzamine, an irreversible alpha-blocker (non-competitive).

questions.text: Give an example of an essential drug.

questions.text: Mention the difference between tolerance and tachyphylaxis.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Tachyphylaxis is acute tolerance not overcome by higher doses.
questions.modelAnswer: Tachyphylaxis is an acute (rapid) tolerance in which the same effect cannot be restored even by a higher dose, for example the tolerance that develops after a few doses of ephedrine due to depletion of stored norepinephrine. Ordinary tolerance develops gradually and can usually be overcome by a higher dose.

questions.text: A patient in shock is given isoprenaline. The nurse expects this drug to increase heart rate. Explain why.
questions.explanation: Beta1 direct stimulation plus beta2-mediated reflex tachycardia raise heart rate.
questions.keyConcept: Isoprenaline raises heart rate via direct beta1 and reflex beta2 effects.
questions.modelAnswer: Isoprenaline is an agonist on beta1 and beta2 receptors. Beta1 stimulation produces positive chronotropic and inotropic effects, markedly increasing cardiac output. Beta2 stimulation causes bronchodilation and vasodilation, which lowers blood pressure and triggers a reflex increase in heart rate. The result is a marked rise in heart rate from both direct and reflex effects.

questions.text: Compare between ion channel receptors and G-protein linked receptors with examples.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Ion-channel receptors gate ions directly; GPCRs act through second messengers.
questions.modelAnswer: In ion-channel receptors, binding of the agonist regulates the opening of the channel, changing membrane potential or intracellular ion concentration to produce the action (e.g., GABA receptors gating Cl- channels and nicotinic N receptors gating Na+/K+ channels). In G-protein linked receptors, the ligand binds and the G-protein regulates the activity of several effectors such as adenylyl cyclase and phospholipase C (e.g., Gs at beta receptors raising cAMP, Gi at alpha-2 and M2 lowering cAMP, and Gq at alpha-1, M1 and M3 producing DAG and IP3).

questions.text: Compare between receptors linked to tyrosine kinase and receptors regulating transcription, with examples.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Tyrosine kinase receptors autophosphorylate; nuclear receptors alter gene transcription.
questions.modelAnswer: Tyrosine kinase-linked receptors have an extracellular part that binds the drug and an intracellular enzymatic (tyrosine kinase) part that undergoes autophosphorylation to produce the action (e.g., insulin receptors). Receptors regulating transcription are intracellular/nuclear receptors that the drug enters the cell to bind, affecting transcription and changing protein production (e.g., steroid hormones such as cortisone and androgens, and vitamin D).

questions.explanation: Intracellular receptors that regulate gene transcription produce effects over hours, the slowest of all receptor classes.
questions.keyConcept: Transcription-regulating (nuclear) receptors are the slowest acting.

questions.text: Which of the following receptor types mediate the slowest transmission of impulses?
questions.explanation: Intracellular receptors that regulate gene transcription act over hours — the slowest signalling; ion channels are the fastest.
questions.keyConcept: Transcription-regulating receptors are the slowest.

questions.text: Compare between competitive and non-competitive antagonists in terms of Emax and EC50.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Competitive shifts EC50; non-competitive lowers Emax.
questions.modelAnswer: A competitive antagonist causes no change in Emax (no change in efficacy) but increases the EC50 (decreased potency). A non-competitive antagonist decreases the Emax (decreased efficacy) with no change in EC50.

questions.text: Complete: define ED50 in the graded dose-response curve and give an example of an essential drug.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: ED50 is the dose giving 50% of maximal effect; paracetamol is an essential drug.
questions.modelAnswer: The ED50 in a graded dose-response curve is the dose that produces 50% of the maximum therapeutic effect. An example of an essential drug is paracetamol.

questions.text: Define ED50 in a graded dose-response curve.
questions.explanation: ED50 marks the dose giving half the maximal graded response and reflects potency.
questions.keyConcept: Graded ED50 is the dose producing 50% of the maximal effect.
questions.modelAnswer: In a graded dose-response curve, the ED50 is the dose that produces 50% of the maximum therapeutic effect.

questions.text: Define therapeutic index and mention its significance.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Therapeutic index = LD50/ED50; larger means safer.
questions.modelAnswer: The therapeutic index is the ratio between the LD50 and the ED50 (LD50/ED50). It indicates the safety of a drug: a large therapeutic index (LD50 much higher than ED50) means the drug is relatively safe.

questions.text: Define therapeutic index and mention its significance. Enumerate 2 drugs with low therapeutic index.
questions.explanation: TI quantifies the safety window between effective and toxic doses.
questions.keyConcept: Therapeutic index = LD50/ED50 and indicates drug safety.
questions.modelAnswer: Definition: the therapeutic index (TI) compares the dose producing a toxic effect to the dose producing a therapeutic effect, calculated as LD50/ED50. Significance: it indicates a drug's safety margin; a larger TI means a safer drug because there is a wider gap between effective and toxic doses. Drugs with low therapeutic index: warfarin, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline (any two).

questions.text: Enumerate 4 factors affecting the dose response relationship.
questions.explanation: Both drug-handling and receptor-level factors shape the response.
questions.keyConcept: Dose response depends on PK, PD, patient and interaction factors.
questions.modelAnswer: Pharmacokinetic factors: affect drug concentration at the site of action (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion). Pharmacodynamic factors: changes at the receptor level (receptor number, sensitivity, post-receptor events). Patient-related factors: age, genetic factors (pharmacogenetics), pathological states such as liver or kidney disease. Drug interactions: synergism, antagonism or potentiation altering responses.

questions.text: Enumerate the difference between competitive and non-competitive antagonists in terms of the shift of the dose-response curve.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Competitive = parallel right shift; non-competitive = downward shift.
questions.modelAnswer: A competitive antagonist produces a parallel shift of the dose-response curve to the right. A non-competitive antagonist produces a non-parallel (downward) shift.

questions.text: Enumerate two drugs with a low therapeutic index.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Lithium, theophylline, aminoglycosides and hypoglycemics have narrow therapeutic indices.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include aminoglycosides, hypoglycemic agents, lithium and theophylline.

questions.text: List four factors that could affect drug response.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Dose, age, sex and disease state are key determinants of drug response.
questions.modelAnswer: Factors include dose, age, sex, pathological states, tolerance, psychological factors, drug interactions and patient compliance.

questions.text: A 55-year-old woman with congestive heart failure is to be treated with a diuretic. Drugs X and Y have the same mechanism of diuretic action. Drug X at 5 mg produces the same magnitude of diuresis as 500 mg of drug Y. This suggests that:
questions.explanation: The same effect at 5 mg versus 500 mg means drug X is ~100 times more potent; equal maximal effect means equal efficacy.
questions.keyConcept: Lower equi-effective dose indicates greater potency.
options: Drug Y is less efficacious than drug X
Drug X is about 100 times more potent than drug Y
Toxicity of drug X is less than that of drug Y
Drug X is a safer drug than drug Y

questions.explanation: 5 mg of X equals 500 mg of Y for the same effect, so X is about 100 times more potent. Equal effect means equal efficacy; potency says nothing about safety or duration.

Caffeine is the least effective and least potent one
d-amphetamine is the drug of choice

questions.text: Drug X and Drug Y are antihypertensive agents. Drug X in the maximum prescribing dose reduces blood pressure by 30 mmHg. Drug Y in the maximum prescribing dose reduces blood pressure of the same patient by 20 mmHg. Therefore:
questions.explanation: Efficacy is the maximal achievable effect. Drug X achieves a greater maximal fall in blood pressure (30 vs 20 mmHg), so Drug Y is less efficacious. The data say nothing about potency, toxicity, or duration.
questions.keyConcept: Efficacy = maximal achievable effect (Emax).
options: Drug Y is less efficacious than drug X
Drug X is more potent than drug Y
Toxicity of drug X is less than that of drug Y
Drug X will have a shorter duration of action than drug Y

questions.text: Drugs X and Y are antihypertensive agents. Drug X at the maximum prescribing dose reduces blood pressure by 30 mmHg. Drug Y at the maximum prescribing dose reduces blood pressure of the same patient by 20 mmHg. Therefore:
questions.explanation: A smaller maximal effect (20 vs 30 mmHg) reflects lower efficacy, so drug Y is less efficacious; this comparison says nothing about potency.
questions.keyConcept: A lower maximal effect indicates lower efficacy.
options: Drug Y is less efficacious than drug X
Drug X is more potent than drug Y

questions.text: Drugs X and Y are antihypertensives. At the maximum prescribing dose, drug X reduces blood pressure by 30 mmHg and drug Y reduces it by 20 mmHg in the same patient. Therefore:

questions.text: Drugs X and Y are oral hypoglycaemic agents. Drug X at 50 mg reduces serum glucose by 50 mg/dl; Drug Y at 5 mg reduces serum glucose by 50 mg/dl. Therefore:
questions.explanation: Drug X requires a higher dose than Drug Y for the same effect, indicating Drug X is less potent.
questions.keyConcept: A higher dose for the same effect means lower potency.
options: Drug X is less efficacious than drug Y
Drug X is less potent than drug Y
Toxicity of drug Y is less than that of drug X
Drug Y will have a shorter duration of action than drug X

questions.text: Drugs X and Y are oral hypoglycemic agents. Drug X at 50 mg reduces serum blood glucose by 50 mg/dl. Drug Y at 5 mg reduces serum blood glucose by 50 mg/dl. Therefore:
questions.explanation: Drug Y achieves the same effect at one-tenth the dose, so drug X is less potent; equal effect size means equal efficacy.

options: Drug X is less efficacious than drug Y

Drug Y will have a shorter duration of action than drug X

questions.text: Drugs X and Y are oral hypoglycemic agents. Drug X at a dose of 50 mg reduces the serum blood glucose by 50 mg/dl. Drug Y at a dose of 5 mg reduces the serum blood glucose by 50 mg/dl. Therefore:

questions.keyConcept: Lower effective dose = greater potency (equal effect = equal efficacy).
options: Drug X is less efficacious than drug Y

X is the most potent & most effective one

questions.text: If the therapeutic index (TI) of drug X is 5 and the TI of drug Y is 10, which of the following is correct?

questions.keyConcept: Tachyphylaxis is acute, dose-irreversible tolerance.

questions.text: A 14-year-old female with asthma treated for 4 months with salbutamol no longer responds to it. Explain the likely reason.
questions.explanation: Chronic beta2-agonist use down-regulates beta2 receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Long-term salbutamol causes beta2 receptor down-regulation (tolerance).
questions.modelAnswer: Tolerance has developed on long-term systemic use due to beta2-receptor down-regulation, so the same dose of salbutamol now produces a reduced bronchodilator response.

questions.text: Compare between intolerance and side effect as augmented adverse effects.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Intolerance occurs below therapeutic dose; side effects occur at therapeutic dose.
questions.modelAnswer: Intolerance is an adverse effect appearing at doses below the therapeutic dose because of a lowered threshold to a normal pharmacologic action (e.g., tinnitus after a single small dose of aspirin). A side effect occurs at the therapeutic dose and may be a primary pharmacological action (dry mouth from antihistamines) or a secondary action (oral thrush from candida overgrowth while taking antibiotics).

questions.text: Compare between overdose and toxicity as augmented adverse effects.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Overdose = slightly above therapeutic; toxicity = very high doses.
questions.modelAnswer: Overdose effects occur at doses slightly above the therapeutic dose (e.g., seizures with lidocaine). Toxic effects occur at very high doses (e.g., hepatotoxicity with acetaminophen).

questions.text: Define drug tolerance and mention its mechanisms.
questions.explanation: Tolerance arises from altered drug levels or altered receptor responsiveness.
questions.keyConcept: Tolerance can be pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic.
questions.modelAnswer: Definition: drug tolerance is a reduced responsiveness to a drug after repeated administration, requiring higher doses to produce the same effect. Mechanisms: pharmacokinetic tolerance (decreased drug concentration at the site of action, e.g. due to enzyme induction) and pharmacodynamic tolerance (changes at the receptor or post-receptor level, e.g. decreased receptor sensitivity or down-regulation).

questions.text: Define idiosyncratic drug adverse effects. Mention 2 examples.
questions.explanation: Idiosyncratic reactions stem from individual genetic/metabolic traits.
questions.keyConcept: Idiosyncratic reactions are unpredictable and genetically determined.
questions.modelAnswer: Definition: idiosyncratic adverse effects are unpredictable, often dose-independent reactions occurring in a small subset of individuals due to genetic predispositions or metabolic abnormalities, and are unrelated to the drug's known pharmacology. Examples: succinylcholine apnoea (prolonged paralysis in atypical plasma cholinesterase); malignant hyperthermia (inherited reaction to certain anaesthetics and neuromuscular blockers); haemolytic anaemia in G6PD-deficient patients triggered by drugs such as primaquine or sulphonamides.

questions.text: Define idiosyncratic drug adverse effects with two examples.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal drug response.
questions.modelAnswer: Idiosyncratic adverse effects are genetically mediated, abnormal responses to a drug, such as the reactions seen in porphyria and favism (G6PD deficiency).

questions.text: Discuss 2 different mechanisms of pharmacodynamic tolerance with examples.
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamic tolerance reflects receptor adaptation or compensatory physiology.
questions.keyConcept: PD tolerance arises from receptor down-regulation and counter-regulation.
questions.modelAnswer: Decreased sensitivity or number of receptors (down-regulation): prolonged agonist exposure decreases receptor number or responsiveness, e.g. long-term beta2-agonists such as salbutamol causing beta2 receptor down-regulation. Counter-regulatory mechanisms: the body's physiological systems adapt to oppose the drug, e.g. chronic vasodilator use prompting salt and water retention that restores blood pressure and reduces effectiveness.

questions.text: Discuss the types of augmented adverse effects and their characters.
questions.explanation: Type A reactions are predictable extensions of the drug's pharmacology.
questions.keyConcept: Augmented (Type A) reactions are dose-dependent and predictable.
questions.modelAnswer: Augmented (Type A) adverse drug reactions are predictable, dose-dependent effects that exaggerate the drug's known pharmacology. They are common, often mild but can be serious, and relate to the drug's primary or secondary pharmacological actions. Example: bleeding with warfarin due to excessive anticoagulation.

questions.text: Enumerate two causes of a bizarre adverse reaction.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Bizarre reactions stem from allergy, immune, genetic or idiosyncratic causes.
questions.modelAnswer: Causes include hypersensitivity (allergy), immune-based (acquired) reactions, genetically based reactions and idiosyncrasy.

questions.text: Enumerate two diseases that can result from continuous use of some drugs.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Chronic drug use can cause hypertension, diabetes or analgesic nephropathy.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include hypertension, diabetes mellitus and analgesic nephropathy.

questions.text: List two examples of pharmacogenetic disorders that could affect drug response.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Acetylation polymorphism and G6PD deficiency are classic pharmacogenetic disorders.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include acetylation polymorphism, hemolytic anemia due to G6PD deficiency, porphyria, succinylcholine (scoline) apnea, malignant hyperthermia, steroid-induced raised intraocular pressure and genetic resistance to anticoagulants.

questions.text: Mention two drugs used against drug allergy.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine, corticosteroids and antihistamines treat drug allergy.
questions.modelAnswer: Epinephrine, corticosteroids and antihistaminics are used to treat drug allergy.

questions.text: State the difference between tolerance and tachyphylaxis.
questions.explanation: Tachyphylaxis is rapid and dose-resistant; tolerance is gradual.
questions.keyConcept: Tachyphylaxis develops fast and cannot be overcome by higher doses.
questions.modelAnswer: Onset: tolerance is gradual, developing over days or weeks, while tachyphylaxis is rapid, developing acutely within minutes to hours. Overcome by increasing dose: tolerance can usually be overcome by increasing the dose, while tachyphylaxis cannot. Mechanism: tolerance commonly involves receptor down-regulation or enzyme induction, while tachyphylaxis commonly involves neurotransmitter depletion (e.g. ephedrine).

questions.text: Sudden withdrawal of drugs may precipitate adverse effects. Discuss this statement with 2 examples.
questions.explanation: Chronic adaptation makes abrupt withdrawal dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers, clonidine or steroids causes rebound effects.
questions.modelAnswer: Sudden cessation of certain drugs can cause severe rebound or withdrawal phenomena because the body has adapted to chronic drug presence. Examples: beta-blockers, where abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension, tachycardia or worsening angina due to beta-receptor up-regulation; clonidine, where sudden stoppage causes severe rebound hypertension and sympathetic overactivity; corticosteroids, where abrupt withdrawal causes acute adrenal insufficiency, hypotension and hypoglycaemia from HPA-axis suppression.

questions.text: What are the measures against drug allergy?
questions.explanation: These agents treat and control allergic and anaphylactic reactions.
questions.keyConcept: Drug allergy is managed with adrenaline, corticosteroids and antihistamines.
questions.modelAnswer: Epinephrine, corticosteroids, and antihistaminics.

questions.text: Cross match each adverse drug reaction type to its example.
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity is immune-mediated (penicillin anaphylaxis); idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal response (barbiturate porphyria); mutagenicity causes gene mutations; teratogenicity causes fetal malformation; iatrogenic disease is drug-induced disease.
questions.keyConcept: Categories of adverse drug reactions: hypersensitivity, idiosyncrasy, mutagenicity, teratogenicity, iatrogenic.

questions.text: Cross match each drug to its potential drug interaction.
questions.explanation: Rifampicin is an enzyme inducer; erythromycin a CYP inhibitor; sulfonamides displace bilirubin; aspirin displaces warfarin; tetracyclines chelate divalent/trivalent cations.
questions.keyConcept: Interaction mechanisms: enzyme induction/inhibition, protein-binding displacement, chelation.

pairs.target: Risk of pregnancy from increased metabolism of oral contraceptives
Theophylline toxicity from inhibition of its metabolism
Kernicterus in the newborn from displacement of bilirubin
Bleeding with warfarin from displacement from plasma proteins
Chelation of Ca²⁺ and Al³⁺ in antacids

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal.
questions.explanation: Abrupt withdrawal causes: alcohol - convulsions; corticosteroids - hypoglycaemia (adrenal insufficiency); beta-blockers - rebound angina; warfarin - rebound thromboembolism; clonidine - rebound hypertension.
questions.keyConcept: Sudden drug withdrawal can cause rebound adverse effects.

pairs.target: Anxiety and convulsions
Hypoglycaemia
Angina
Thromboembolism
Hypertension

questions.text: Cross match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it.
questions.explanation: Barbiturates precipitate acute porphyria; succinylcholine triggers malignant hyperthermia/apnea (pseudocholinesterase deficiency); corticosteroids raise IOP in susceptible eyes; isoniazid causes neuropathy/hepatitis in slow acetylators.
questions.keyConcept: Pharmacogenetic disorders unmasked by specific drugs.

pairs.target: Barbiturates
Succinylcholine
Corticosteroids

pairs.premise: Increased risk of neuropathy and hepatitis in slow acetylators
pairs.target: Isoniazid

questions.explanation: Intolerance is an exaggerated response at low doses; cross-tolerance extends to related drugs; tolerance is gradual and dose-reversible; tachyphylaxis is rapid and dose-resistant.
questions.keyConcept: Distinguish intolerance, tolerance, cross-tolerance, and tachyphylaxis.

Tolerance to a related drug from the same group
Reduced responsiveness on repeated intake, overcome by increasing the dose

questions.keyConcept: Distinguishing intolerance, tolerance, cross tolerance, and tachyphylaxis.

Reduced responsiveness on repeated intake; overcome by increasing the dose

questions.text: Cross match each type of adverse drug reaction to its example.
questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity = immune anaphylaxis (penicillins); idiosyncrasy = genetically determined abnormal response (porphyria with barbiturates); mutagenicity = gene damage; teratogenicity = fetal malformation; iatrogenic = physician/drug-induced disease.
questions.keyConcept: Classifying adverse drug reactions by mechanism.

pairs.target: Anaphylaxis with penicillins
Precipitation of porphyria with barbiturates
Gene abnormalities with metronidazole
Cleft palate with antiepileptics
Peptic ulcer with aspirin

questions.text: Cross match the following terms with their corresponding definition.
questions.explanation: Idiosyncrasy = genetically abnormal response (succinylcholine apnea); mutagenicity = gene damage; teratogenicity = fetal malformation; iatrogenic = physician/drug-induced disease; hypersensitivity = immune anaphylaxis.
questions.keyConcept: Classifying adverse reactions by mechanism.

Drug induced gene abnormalities
Fetal abnormalities due to taking during 1st trimester of pregnancy
Aspirin induced peptic ulcer (disease)

questions.text: Cross-match the following to the corresponding definition.
questions.explanation: Idiosyncrasy is a genetically determined abnormal response; mutagenicity induces genetic abnormalities; teratogenicity causes foetal malformations; iatrogenic effects result from treatment; hypersensitivity is an immune reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Adverse drug effects fall into distinct mechanistic categories.

pairs.target: Apnoea due to administration of succinylcholine
Drug induced gene abnormalities
Foetal abnormalities due to taking during 1st trimester of pregnancy
Aspirin induced peptic ulcer disease

questions.text: Cross match the following tolerance/response terms by their corresponding definition.
questions.explanation: Intolerance = exaggerated response at low dose; cross tolerance = extends to related drugs; idiosyncrasy = genetically determined abnormal response; tachyphylaxis = rapid tolerance not overcome by dose increase; tolerance = gradual decreased response overcome by dose increase.
questions.keyConcept: Intolerance, cross tolerance, idiosyncrasy, tachyphylaxis, tolerance.

questions.text: Cross match the type of interaction occurring on co-administration of the following drugs.
questions.explanation: Sulfonamides + trimethoprim block sequential folate synthesis steps (synergism); two sedatives give summation; β-lactamase inhibitors are not antibacterial alone but potentiate ampicillin.
questions.keyConcept: Drug-interaction types: summation, synergism, potentiation.

Summation (additive effect of like drugs)
Potentiation (inactive drug enhances the active one)

questions.explanation: Essential drugs meet priority health needs; orphan drugs treat rare diseases; OTC drugs need no prescription; mutagenic drugs alter genes; teratogenic drugs harm the foetus.
questions.keyConcept: Drug categories are defined by their use and risk profile.

questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Decreased response on repeated administration is TOLERANCE, not intolerance (which is an exaggerated response at low doses); D is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Intolerance = exaggerated low-dose response, not decreased response on repetition.
options: Side effect of the drug is dose dependent adverse effect
Pharmacogenecity is a dose independent adverse effect
Iatrogenic disease is a disease due to using drug
Intolerance is decrease response of the drug due to repeated administration
Drug allergy occurs due to prior exposure to a drug act as antigen

questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Behind-the-counter drugs are dispensed under pharmacist supervision but do not necessarily require direct patient consultation, so this description is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: BTC drugs are dispensed under pharmacist supervision.
options: Prescription-only medications (POM) are only dispensed with a prescription
Over-the-counter drugs (OTC) can be dispensed without a prescription
Behind-the-counter drugs (BTC) are only dispensed with the pharmacist or the patient
Noncompliance is one of the factors that can modify the drug response

questions.text: Choose the incorrect statement:
questions.explanation: Intolerance is an exaggerated response to a normal dose, not a decreased response from repeated administration (which is tolerance), so this is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Intolerance is an exaggerated, not reduced, response.
options: Side effect of the drug is a dose-dependent adverse effect
Pharmacogenicity is a dose-independent adverse effect
Iatrogenic disease is a disease due to using a drug
Intolerance is a decreased response to the drug due to repeated administration
Drug allergy occurs due to prior exposure to a drug functioning as an antigen

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Alcohol:
questions.explanation: Abrupt alcohol withdrawal causes a hyperexcitable state with anxiety, tremor and seizures.
questions.keyConcept: Alcohol withdrawal causes anxiety and convulsions.

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Beta-blockers:
questions.explanation: Abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal causes rebound receptor up-regulation, precipitating angina (and possibly infarction).
questions.keyConcept: Beta-blocker withdrawal precipitates rebound angina.

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Clonidine:
questions.explanation: Sudden clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension from a surge in sympathetic outflow.
questions.keyConcept: Clonidine withdrawal causes rebound hypertension.

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Corticosteroids:
questions.explanation: Sudden corticosteroid withdrawal causes acute adrenal insufficiency, which can present with hypoglycemia.
questions.keyConcept: Steroid withdrawal causes adrenal insufficiency (hypoglycemia).

questions.text: Cross-match each drug to the adverse effect that may follow its sudden withdrawal - Warfarin:
questions.explanation: Stopping warfarin abruptly leaves a transient hypercoagulable state, increasing thromboembolism risk.
questions.keyConcept: Warfarin withdrawal risks rebound thromboembolism.

questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it - Increased risk of neuropathy in slow acetylators:
questions.explanation: Slow acetylators metabolise isoniazid slowly, leading to accumulation and peripheral neuropathy.
questions.keyConcept: Isoniazid causes neuropathy in slow acetylators.

questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it - Malignant hyperthermia or apnea:
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine can trigger malignant hyperthermia and, in pseudocholinesterase deficiency, prolonged apnea.
questions.keyConcept: Succinylcholine reveals malignant hyperthermia / apnea.

questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it - Precipitation of porphyria:
questions.explanation: Barbiturates induce hepatic ALA synthase and can precipitate acute porphyria.
questions.keyConcept: Barbiturates can precipitate acute porphyria.

questions.text: Cross-match each pharmacogenetic disorder to the drug that might reveal it - Raised intraocular pressure:
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids can raise intraocular pressure in genetically susceptible (steroid-responder) individuals.
questions.keyConcept: Corticosteroids can raise intraocular pressure.

questions.text: Oral thrush that may occur with prolonged use of broad spectrum antibacterial drugs is:
questions.explanation: Oral thrush from broad-spectrum antibiotics is a superinfection — an indirect (secondary) pharmacological side effect resulting from suppression of normal flora.
questions.keyConcept: Antibiotic superinfection is a secondary (2nd) pharmacological effect.

questions.text: Oral thrush that may occur with prolonged use of broad-spectrum antibacterial drugs is:
questions.explanation: Superinfection (oral thrush) results indirectly from killing normal flora, a secondary pharmacological side effect rather than a direct action of the drug.
questions.keyConcept: Superinfection is a secondary pharmacological side effect.

questions.text: Pharmacokinetic tolerance may occur due to all the following except:
questions.explanation: A change in receptor number is a pharmacodynamic mechanism; reduced absorption/delivery and increased elimination are pharmacokinetic causes of tolerance.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor-number change is pharmacodynamic, not pharmacokinetic, tolerance.
options: Decrease delivery of the drug to its receptors
Decrease number of receptors of the drugs
Increase elimination of the drug by enzyme inducers

questions.text: Pharmacokinetic tolerance may occur due to all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: A decrease in receptor number is pharmacodynamic, not pharmacokinetic, tolerance, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Receptor down-regulation is pharmacodynamic tolerance.
options: Decrease in delivery of the drug to its receptors
Decrease in the number of receptors of the drug
Increased elimination of the drug by enzyme inducers

questions.text: Teratogenicity means:
questions.explanation: Teratogenicity refers to the induction of fetal abnormalities, classically when a drug is taken during the first trimester.
questions.keyConcept: Teratogenicity = first-trimester drug-induced fetal malformation.
options: Apnea due to administration of succinylcholine
Anaphylactic shock due to intravenous injection of penicillin
Induction of fetal abnormalities due to taking a drug during the first trimester of pregnancy

questions.text: The following are possible causes of pharmacodynamic tolerance except:
questions.explanation: Altered delivery of drug to its site is a pharmacokinetic mechanism; receptor sensitivity/number and neurotransmitter level changes are pharmacodynamic.
questions.keyConcept: Drug delivery changes cause pharmacokinetic (not pharmacodynamic) tolerance.
options: Change in the sensitivity of receptors
Change in the number of receptors
Change in the delivery of drug to site of action
Change in the level of neurotransmitters

questions.text: The following are possible causes of pharmacodynamic tolerance EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Changes in drug delivery to the site of action are pharmacokinetic, not pharmacodynamic, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Pharmacodynamic tolerance is receptor-level, not delivery-level.
options: Change in the sensitivity of receptors
Change in the number of receptors
Change in the delivery of the drug to its site of access
Change in the level of neurotransmitter actions

questions.text: Which of the following is the definition of tachyphylaxis?
questions.explanation: Tachyphylaxis is an acute, rapidly developing unresponsiveness that cannot be overcome by increasing the dose.
questions.keyConcept: Tachyphylaxis is acute tolerance unresponsive to dose increases.
options: Lower threshold to a normal pharmacologic action
Tolerance to a related drug from the same group
Reduced responsiveness on repeated intake, overcome by increasing the dose
Acute non-responsiveness to a drug, not overcome by increasing the dose

questions.text: Which of the following means teratogenicity?
questions.explanation: Teratogenicity is the capacity of a drug to induce fetal malformations, especially during organogenesis in the first trimester.
questions.keyConcept: Teratogenicity = drug-induced fetal abnormalities.
options: Immune-based adverse reactions occurring with second exposure to the drug

questions.text: Intrinsic activity is a drug's ability to elicit:
questions.explanation: Intrinsic activity (efficacy) is the ability of a drug, once bound to its receptor, to activate it and produce a biological response. Binding affinity is a separate property; a drug can bind strongly yet have no intrinsic activity (a pure antagonist).
questions.keyConcept: Intrinsic activity (efficacy) = ability to produce a response after binding.

questions.text: Regarding an inverse agonist, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: An inverse agonist has affinity for the receptor and possesses (negative) intrinsic efficacy, producing an effect opposite to that of the agonist by reducing constitutive receptor activity. In tissues lacking constitutive activity it behaves like a competitive antagonist, so both B and C are correct.
questions.keyConcept: Inverse agonists have affinity and negative efficacy; act as antagonists when there is no constitutive activity.
options: In the absence of the agonist, it blocks the empty receptor
It is considered pharmacologically as an antagonist

questions.text: Alpha methyldopa: mechanism of action and therapeutic use.
questions.explanation: Central alpha2 stimulation reduces sympathetic drive.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa is a central alpha2 agonist used in pregnancy hypertension.
questions.modelAnswer: Mechanism: a prodrug metabolised to alpha-methyl noradrenaline, which acts as a false neurotransmitter and stimulates central alpha2 adrenoceptors, reducing sympathetic outflow from the brainstem and lowering peripheral vascular resistance and heart rate. Therapeutic use: hypertension, particularly first-line for hypertension in pregnancy.

questions.text: Beta blockers are used as prophylaxis in esophageal varices. Explain.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Non-selective beta blockers lower portal pressure via splanchnic vasoconstriction and reduced cardiac output.
questions.modelAnswer: Non-selective beta blockers reduce portal blood flow by causing splanchnic vasoconstriction (through beta-2 blockade) and by reducing cardiac output (through beta-1 blockade).

questions.text: Carvedilol is used in chronic heart failure. Explain.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
