questions.keyConcept: Dose- and receptor-dependent hemodynamics of dopaminergic/adrenergic agonists.

pairs.target: Increases blood pressure with reflex vagal bradycardia
Renal vasodilator, positive inotrope and chronotrope, with vasopressor effects at high dose
Positive inotrope with minimal effect on blood pressure or heart rate
Weak positive inotrope and powerful splanchnic vasodilator

questions.text: Cross match each sympathomimetic to its therapeutic use.
questions.explanation: Terbutaline/ritodrine (β2) relax the uterus; epinephrine (α) is a local hemostatic; oxymetazoline (α) is a topical decongestant; pseudoephedrine (mixed) is a systemic decongestant.
questions.keyConcept: Therapeutic uses of selective and mixed sympathomimetics.

pairs.target: β2 agonist used in premature labor / threatened abortion
Directly acting hemostatic in epistaxis
α agonist topical nasal decongestant
Dual-acting systemic nasal decongestant

questions.text: Cross match the following adrenergic drug classes to their indications:
questions.explanation: β2 agonists treat asthma and tocolysis; β1 agonists support failing hearts; α1 agonists are decongestant/mydriatic; central α2 agonists lower blood pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Indications mapped to adrenergic receptor-agonist classes.

pairs.target: Asthma / threatened abortion / premature labor
Chronic refractory HF / acute HF / cardiogenic shock
Fundus examination / allergic conjunctivitis
Hypertension

questions.text: Cross-match the following adrenergic drugs to their indications.
questions.explanation: Beta1 agonists stimulate the failing heart; beta2 agonists relax bronchi and uterus; alpha1 agonists cause mydriasis and conjunctival decongestion; central alpha2 agonists lower blood pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenergic agonists are used according to their receptor selectivity.

pairs.target: Chronic refractory HF / acute HF / cardiogenic shock
Asthma / threatened abortion / premature labour
Fundus examination / allergic conjunctivitis
Hypertension

questions.text: Cross match the following inotrope/vasoactive sympathomimetics to their hemodynamic effects:
questions.explanation: Phenylephrine (α1) raises BP with reflex bradycardia; dopamine is dose-dependent (renal vasodilation → inotropy → vasopressor); dobutamine is a β1 inotrope; dopexamine is a weak inotrope and splanchnic vasodilator.
questions.keyConcept: Hemodynamic profiles of phenylephrine, dopamine, dobutamine and dopexamine.

pairs.target: Increase blood pressure with reflex vagal bradycardia
Renal vasodilator, positive inotrope & chronotrope with vasopressor effects in high dose
Positive inotrope, minimal effect on blood pressure or heart rate
Weak positive inotrope; powerful splanchnic vasodilator

questions.text: Cross match the following sympathomimetics to their hemodynamic effects:
questions.explanation: NE (α1/β1) markedly raises BP with reflex bradycardia; isoprenaline (β1/β2) drops diastolic/mean BP and raises HR; epinephrine raises mean BP and HR; midodrine is an α1 prodrug raising BP with reflex bradycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Hemodynamic signatures of NE, isoprenaline, epinephrine and midodrine.

pairs.target: Marked increase in blood pressure with reflex bradycardia
Decreases diastolic & mean blood pressure & increases heart rate
Increases mean blood pressure & increases heart rate
Prodrug, increases blood pressure with reflex vagal bradycardia

questions.text: Cross match the following sympathomimetics to their uses:
questions.explanation: Terbutaline/ritodrine are β2 tocolytics; epinephrine is a hemostatic vasoconstrictor; oxymetazoline is a topical α decongestant; pseudoephedrine is a dual-acting systemic decongestant.
questions.keyConcept: Therapeutic uses of terbutaline/ritodrine, epinephrine, oxymetazoline and pseudoephedrine.

pairs.target: Beta2 agonist in premature labor / threatened abortion
Directly acting hemostatic in epistaxis
Alpha agonist topical nasal decongestant
Dual acting systemic nasal decongestant

questions.text: All the following drugs induce tachycardia except:
questions.explanation: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha1 agonist that causes vasoconstriction and a reflex bradycardia, so it does not induce tachycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylephrine causes reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia.

questions.text: All the following regarding adrenaline is true except:
questions.explanation: Adrenaline increases both systolic and diastolic blood pressure, raising mean BP, so 'no change' is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline raises mean arterial pressure.
options: Should be avoided with beta blockers, thyrotoxicosis or ischaemic heart disease
Relaxation of the wall of the GIT by stimulation of alpha and beta receptors
No change in mean BP in therapeutic dose

questions.text: Alpha1 receptor agonist is not effective in treatment of:
questions.explanation: Alpha1 agonists cause vasoconstriction; ventricular tachycardia with hypotension requires increased contractility or rate, not vasoconstriction.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha1 agonists do not treat ventricular tachycardia.

questions.text: Alpha1 receptor agonist should not be used in the following condition:
questions.explanation: Alpha1 agonists cause vasoconstriction and raise blood pressure, so they should not be used in a hypertensive state.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha1 agonists are contraindicated in hypertension.
options: Fundus examination in patients with glaucoma

questions.text: Dobutamine differs from dopamine in all the following except:
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is preferred in acute heart failure without renal dysfunction; dopamine is preferred when there is renal dysfunction, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine, not dobutamine, is preferred with renal dysfunction.
options: Preferred in acute heart failure with renal dysfunction
Inotropic effect more than chronotropic effect

questions.text: Dopamine is preferred to dobutamine in cardiogenic shock with hypotension or renal impairment because:
questions.explanation: Dopamine improves renal perfusion (D1) and supports BP via α vasopressor effect, making it preferable when hypotension/renal impairment coexist (A and B).
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine adds D1 renal vasodilation and α vasopressor support over dobutamine.
options: D-1 effect of dopamine induces renal vasodilation & increases renal blood flow
Beta-1 effect of dobutamine increases arrhythmia compared to dopamine

questions.text: Dopamine is preferred to dobutamine in cardiogenic shock with hypotension or renal impairment because:
questions.explanation: Dopamine's D1 agonism increases renal blood flow while its alpha-mediated vasoconstriction supports blood pressure, making it useful in shock with renal impairment.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine combines renal vasodilatation with vasopressor support.
options: D1 stimulant effect of dopamine induces vasodilatation and increases renal blood flow
Dopamine induces an alpha-mediated vasopressor effect
Beta1 selective effect of dobutamine increases the risk of arrhythmia compared to dopamine

questions.text: Epinephrine induced hypokalemia is due to:
questions.explanation: Per the source key the answer is A+B. Note: epinephrine-induced hypokalemia is primarily due to β2-mediated cellular (skeletal muscle/hepatic) K+ uptake, so the option wording is pharmacologically imperfect — flag for review.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine causes β2-mediated cellular K+ uptake (item wording flagged).

questions.text: Epinephrine should be avoided in all of the following patients except:
questions.explanation: Per the source key, the exception is patients on alpha blockers. Note: epinephrine with a non-selective α-blocker can cause 'epinephrine reversal,' so this item is pharmacologically debatable — flag for review.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine is hazardous in thyrotoxic/diabetic/hypertensive/cardiac patients (item flagged).

questions.text: In paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia with hypotension, reflex bradycardia may be induced by:
questions.explanation: Phenylephrine raises blood pressure by alpha1 vasoconstriction, triggering a reflex vagal bradycardia useful in PSVT with hypotension.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylephrine ends PSVT through reflex vagal bradycardia.

questions.text: Metabolic actions of epinephrine include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Epinephrine inhibits insulin secretion via α2 (not β2), so C is the exception. Note: the K+ effect (option B) is actually β2-mediated, so that statement is also imperfectly worded — flag for review.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine inhibits insulin via α2 receptors (item has a secondary wording flaw on K+).
options: Decreases serum K by B1 stimulation
Inhibition of Insulin secretion by B2

questions.text: Noradrenaline can be used in all the following types of shock except:
questions.explanation: Noradrenaline is not used in anaphylactic shock; adrenaline is preferred because of its beta2 effects.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline, not noradrenaline, is used in anaphylaxis.
options: Cardiogenic with systolic blood pressure less than 70 mmHg

questions.text: Pharmacological actions of subcutaneous injection of adrenaline do not include:
questions.explanation: Adrenaline stimulates (not decreases) renin release via beta1 receptors, so this statement is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline increases beta1-mediated renin release.
options: Decrease renin release (beta1) decreasing serum potassium

questions.text: Salbutamol replaced epinephrine in treatment of bronchial asthma because:
questions.explanation: Salbutamol is β2-selective with a longer duration (not a MAO/COMT substrate), fewer cardiac effects and multiple routes — but it DOES cause tremor, so all are true except A.
questions.keyConcept: Salbutamol: selective β2 agonist, longer-acting than epinephrine but still causes tremor.
options: It seldom induces tremors or tolerance on long term use
Longer duration of action since it is not metabolized by MAO or COMT
No cardiac complications in regular doses
Can be given by many routes

questions.text: Selective beta2 agonists replaced adrenaline in treatment of bronchial asthma because of all the following except:
questions.explanation: Selective beta2 agonists can still cause tremors and tolerance on long-term use, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Beta2 agonists can still cause tremors and tolerance.
options: Longer duration of action since it is not metabolised by MAO or COMT
It seldom induces tremors or tolerance on long-term use
No cardiac complications in regular doses
Can be given by many routes

questions.text: The following adverse effect is not encountered with selective beta2 agonist:
questions.explanation: Selective beta2 agonists cause hypokalaemia (not hyperkalaemia), so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Beta2 agonists cause hypokalaemia.
options: Tolerance on long-term systemic use due to receptor down-regulation

questions.text: The following adverse effects are seen with both methyl dopa & clonidine:
questions.explanation: Both central α2 agonists cause sedation/dry mouth/sexual dysfunction and bradycardia with fluid retention (A and B); hepatitis/hemolytic anemia/lupus are specific to methyldopa.
questions.keyConcept: Shared central α2-agonist effects of methyldopa and clonidine.
options: Sedation, dry mouth and sexual dysfunction
Bradycardia and salt and water retention

questions.text: The following agent does not act on dopaminergic receptors:
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is a β1 agonist with no dopaminergic activity; dopamine, dopexamine and fenoldopam all act on dopamine receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Dobutamine does not act on dopaminergic receptors.

questions.text: The following agent does not stimulate β1-receptors:
questions.explanation: Per the source key, dopexamine (a β2 and dopaminergic agonist) lacks significant β1 activity. Note: salbutamol is also β2-selective and could be argued — follow the source key.
questions.keyConcept: Dopexamine acts on β2/dopaminergic receptors, not β1.

questions.text: The following agent does not stimulate β2-receptors:
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is a selective β1 agonist with no β2 activity. Ritodrine is a β2 agonist (tocolytic), celiprolol has partial β2-agonist activity, and dopexamine activates β2 receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Dobutamine is β1-selective and lacks β2 activity.

questions.text: The following agent does not stimulate beta1 receptors:
questions.explanation: Dopexamine is a selective beta2 and D1 agonist and does not significantly stimulate beta1 receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Dopexamine acts on beta2 and D1, not beta1.

questions.text: The following agent/s is/are a prodrug:
questions.explanation: Midodrine (→ desglymidodrine) and α-methyldopa (→ α-methylnorepinephrine) are both prodrugs, so C and D.
questions.keyConcept: Midodrine and α-methyldopa are prodrugs.

questions.text: The following are actions mediated by stimulation of alpha1 adrenoceptors except:
questions.explanation: Alpha1 stimulation increases hepatic potassium release through glycogenolysis, it does not decrease it.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha1 stimulation increases hepatic potassium release.
options: Relaxation of walls of the GIT and urinary tracts
Decreases potassium release from the liver
Contraction of prostate and vas deferens

questions.text: The following are actions mediated by stimulation of alpha2 adrenoceptors except:
questions.explanation: Alpha2 adrenoceptor stimulation inhibits renin release; it does not stimulate it.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha2 stimulation inhibits renin release.
options: Central sympathetic outflow decreasing blood pressure

questions.text: The following drug does not act on dopaminergic receptors:
questions.explanation: Dobutamine is a selective beta1 agonist and does not act on dopaminergic receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Dobutamine is beta1-selective, not dopaminergic.

questions.text: The following drugs increase the effect of noradrenaline except:
questions.explanation: Reserpine inhibits vesicular uptake of noradrenaline, depleting its stores and decreasing its effect, unlike the others which enhance it.
questions.keyConcept: Reserpine depletes noradrenaline, reducing its effect.

questions.text: The following indication(s) of adrenaline is/are entirely due to its alpha effect:
questions.explanation: Alpha1-mediated vasoconstriction prolongs local anaesthetics and provides topical haemostasis, whereas anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest involve mixed alpha and beta effects.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline's vasoconstrictor uses are purely alpha-mediated.
options: To prolong the action of local anaesthetics

questions.text: The following indication/s of epinephrine is/are entirely due to its α effect:
questions.explanation: Prolonging local anaesthetic action and stopping epistaxis both rely on α-mediated vasoconstriction; anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest also use β effects.
questions.keyConcept: α-mediated vasoconstriction underlies local-anaesthetic prolongation and epistaxis control.
options: To prolong action of local Anesthetics

questions.text: The following is a dual acting sympathomimetic drug:
questions.explanation: Pseudoephedrine is a dual-acting sympathomimetic, stimulating adrenergic receptors both directly and indirectly.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudoephedrine acts both directly and indirectly.

questions.text: The following is a shared adverse effect between dopamine and dobutamine:
questions.explanation: Per the source answer key the marked answer is hypertension; it is most pronounced with higher-dose dopamine through alpha1 agonism.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine and dobutamine share cardiovascular adverse effects.

questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about adrenaline:
questions.explanation: Adrenaline induces hyperglycaemia via beta2 stimulation (glycogenolysis and decreased insulin release), not hypoglycaemia.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline causes hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia.
options: Used in asthma due to its alpha and beta agonistic effect
Lifesaving in anaphylactic shock due to its rapid action
Induces hypoglycaemia due to its beta2 agonistic effect
Induces hypotension after injection of an alpha blocker

questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about amphetamine (a non-catecholamine indirectly acting sympathomimetic):
questions.explanation: Amphetamine is highly lipophilic and readily enters the CNS (a potent central stimulant), so this statement is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Amphetamine readily crosses into the CNS.
options: Does not readily cross into the CNS

questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about sympathomimetics:
questions.explanation: A directly acting alpha1 agonist causes vasoconstriction and a rise in blood pressure that triggers reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia, so this statement is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha1 agonists cause reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia.
options: Inhibition of vesicular uptake abolishes the effect of indirectly acting drugs
Inhibition of vesicular uptake decreases the effect of dual (mixed) acting drugs
Inhibition of monoamine oxidase increases the effect of indirectly acting drugs
Directly acting alpha1 agonist induces reflex tachycardia

questions.text: The following is incorrect about subcutaneous administration of adrenaline:
questions.explanation: Adrenaline causes alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and relaxation in the GIT, decreasing (not increasing) GIT motility.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline decreases GIT motility.

questions.text: The following is not a character of ephedrine (non-catecholamine sympathomimetic):
questions.explanation: Ephedrine is lipophilic and readily enters the CNS, so this statement is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Ephedrine readily enters the CNS.
options: Not destroyed by MAO and COMT

questions.text: The following is not a pharmacological effect of direct acting beta receptor agonists:
questions.explanation: Beta receptor agonists increase heart rate (positive chronotropy) and cardiac output; they do not decrease heart rate.
questions.keyConcept: Beta agonists raise heart rate, not lower it.
options: Relax smooth muscle of the bronchi

questions.text: The following is not a therapeutic use of indirect sympathomimetic (amphetamine):
questions.explanation: Amphetamine can cause hypertension as a side effect and is not used to treat it.
questions.keyConcept: Amphetamine causes, not treats, hypertension.

questions.text: The following is not a therapeutic use of phenylephrine (selective alpha1 agonist):
questions.explanation: Phenylephrine causes vasoconstriction and is not used in peripheral vascular disease, which requires vasodilatation.
questions.keyConcept: Phenylephrine constricts vessels, so it cannot treat vascular disease.
options: Fundus examination especially in a patient with glaucoma
Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia with marked hypotension

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of salbutamol (beta2 agonist):
questions.explanation: Salbutamol causes hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia; tremors, reflex tachycardia and worsening hypoxaemia are recognised effects.
questions.keyConcept: Beta2 agonists cause hypokalaemia, not hyperkalaemia.

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of selective alpha1 agonist:
questions.explanation: Selective alpha1 agonists cause vasoconstriction with reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha1 agonists cause reflex bradycardia, not tachycardia.

questions.text: The following is not an expected adverse effect of IV infusion of dopamine:
questions.explanation: Dopamine usually causes tachycardia and arrhythmia, not bradycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.

questions.text: The following is not an expected adverse effect of pseudoephedrine:
questions.explanation: Pseudoephedrine causes vasoconstriction and central stimulation; hypotension is not expected, as it tends to raise blood pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudoephedrine raises blood pressure, not lowers it.
options: Urinary retention especially in old males

questions.text: The following is not an indication for indirect sympathomimetics:
questions.explanation: Indirect sympathomimetics often cause hypertension as an adverse effect and are not used to treat it.
questions.keyConcept: Indirect sympathomimetics cause, not treat, hypertension.

questions.text: The following is not an indication of salbutamol (beta2 agonist):
questions.explanation: Salbutamol is used for asthma and to delay premature labour; it does not treat peripheral vascular disease or chronic postural hypotension (C and D).
questions.keyConcept: Salbutamol does not treat vascular or postural hypotension disorders.

questions.text: The following is not correctly matched to its adverse effect:
questions.explanation: Midodrine is an α1 agonist causing hypertension with reflex bradycardia — not hypotension and tachycardia — so D is incorrectly matched.
questions.keyConcept: Midodrine (α1 agonist) causes hypertension with reflex bradycardia.
options: Clonidine / rebound hypertension even on missing a single dose
Bisoprolol / rebound tachycardia & anginal pain on sudden withdrawal

questions.text: Tolerance due to prolonged use of salbutamol is due to:
questions.explanation: Salbutamol tolerance is multifactorial, involving beta2 receptor down-regulation and changes in lung mechanics ('locked lung syndrome').
questions.keyConcept: Salbutamol tolerance has several contributing mechanisms.
options: Decrease in number of beta2 receptors

questions.text: Which of the following can activate dopaminergic as well as adrenergic receptors?
questions.explanation: Dopamine activates dopaminergic (D1), β1 and α1 receptors dose-dependently, and dopexamine activates dopaminergic (D1, D2) and adrenergic β2 receptors. Dobutamine acts only on β1.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine and dopexamine act on both dopaminergic and adrenergic receptors.

questions.text: Which of the following has beta action and can be used in bronchial asthma?
questions.explanation: Salbutamol is a selective beta-2 agonist that produces bronchodilation, making it useful in bronchial asthma.
questions.keyConcept: Salbutamol is a beta-2 selective bronchodilator.

questions.text: Which of the following is a side effect of dopamine?
questions.explanation: Palpitations and anginal pain are common dopamine side effects, especially at higher doses through beta1 stimulation.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine causes palpitations and anginal pain.

questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement?
questions.explanation: Dopamine does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so it cannot be used directly in Parkinsonism; levodopa is used instead.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine cannot cross the BBB to treat Parkinsonism.
options: MAO inhibitors are indicated in parkinsonism
Reserpine depletes stores of noradrenaline and sympathetic outflow
Beta3 agonists relax detrusor muscle and are used in overactive bladder
Dopamine can cross the BBB and is used in Parkinsonism

questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline increases both heart rate and blood pressure (raising mean arterial pressure), so this statement is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Adrenaline raises both heart rate and blood pressure.
options: Stimulation of beta1 and beta3 increases lipolysis
Noradrenaline decreases heart rate and increases blood pressure
Adrenaline increases heart rate and decreases blood pressure
Dobutamine is a selective beta1 agonist
Fenoldopam is a selective dopamine receptor agonist

questions.text: Which of the following is not an indication for indirect sympathomimetics?
questions.explanation: Indirect sympathomimetics are used in narcolepsy, weight reduction and ADHD; they cause hypertension rather than treat it.
questions.keyConcept: Indirect sympathomimetics do not treat hypertension.

questions.text: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of indirect sympathomimetics?
questions.explanation: Indirect sympathomimetics, like amphetamine, act mainly by increasing the release of noradrenaline from presynaptic terminals.
questions.keyConcept: Indirect sympathomimetics increase noradrenaline release.
options: They activate the adrenergic receptor directly
They decrease the degradation of noradrenaline
They activate the down-regulated adrenergic receptor
They increase the release of noradrenaline

questions.text: Which of the following is the mechanism of action of reserpine?
questions.explanation: Reserpine blocks the vesicular uptake of noradrenaline, leading to depletion of noradrenaline stores.
questions.keyConcept: Reserpine blocks vesicular noradrenaline uptake.
options: It blocks uptake I of noradrenaline
It blocks the vesicular uptake of noradrenaline
It is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor

questions.text: Which of the following is wrong regarding mirabegron (beta3 agonist)?
questions.explanation: Mirabegron tends to increase blood pressure and heart rate, so a decrease in blood pressure is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Mirabegron raises, not lowers, blood pressure.
options: May increase the risk of urinary tract infection
May precipitate angioedema in allergic patients

questions.text: Which of the following statement regarding beta adrenergic receptors is not true?
questions.explanation: Isoprenaline is a non-selective beta agonist that causes significant tachycardia, so it is not used to treat tachycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Isoprenaline causes tachycardia and cannot treat it.
options: Dobutamine is a selective beta1 agonist used in acute heart failure
Salbutamol is a selective beta2 agonist used in acute attacks of bronchial asthma
Beta3 agonist is used in hyperactive bladder with a risk of hypertension
Isoprenaline is a non-selective beta agonist used in treatment of tachycardia

questions.text: Atropine is used in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning. Explain, mentioning its dose.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine 2-5 mg every 5 min controls muscarinic effects until atropinization.
questions.modelAnswer: Atropine is used to dry bronchial secretions and stop wheezing; it is given as 2-5 mg every 5 minutes until full atropinization is achieved.

questions.text: Compare and contrast between neostigmine and physostigmine.
questions.explanation: Their key difference is BBB penetration, which determines their clinical roles.
questions.keyConcept: Neostigmine (quaternary) stays peripheral; physostigmine (tertiary) acts centrally.
questions.modelAnswer: Chemical class: neostigmine is a quaternary ammonium compound while physostigmine is a tertiary amine. BBB: neostigmine does not cross the blood-brain barrier while physostigmine does. Routes: neostigmine is given orally or parenterally while physostigmine is given orally, topically (eye) or parenterally. Direct action: neostigmine also has direct nicotinic action on Nm receptors in addition to cholinesterase inhibition while physostigmine is primarily a cholinesterase inhibitor. Clinical use: neostigmine is used for myasthenia gravis, paralytic ileus and as an antidote to neuromuscular blockers, while physostigmine is used for atropine toxicity, glaucoma and (rarely) Alzheimer's disease.

questions.text: Compare between atropine and hyoscine.
questions.explanation: Hyoscine is more central and antiemetic; atropine is more cardiac and longer-acting on the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine is more sedating/antiemetic; atropine is more tachycardic and longer mydriatic.
questions.modelAnswer: CNS effects: atropine has less CNS penetration and may cause excitement at high doses, while hyoscine penetrates the CNS more and causes drowsiness and amnesia. Antiemetic effect: atropine is weak, while hyoscine is potent (used for motion sickness). Mydriatic duration: atropine is longer acting (days), while hyoscine is shorter acting (hours). Cardiovascular effect: atropine causes more prominent tachycardia, while hyoscine has less pronounced cardiovascular effects.

questions.text: Complete the following statements about cholinergic and anticholinergic drugs.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Edrophonium diagnoses myasthenia, donepezil treats Alzheimer's, and atropine is contraindicated in glaucoma/BPH.
questions.modelAnswer: Edrophonium is used in the diagnosis of myasthenia gravis. Donepezil is the neostigmine analogue used in Alzheimer dementia. The effect of atropine on the eye persists for more than 72 hours. Atropine is contraindicated in acute glaucoma and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Pilocarpine is the drug of choice in the treatment of glaucoma, while bethanechol is the drug of choice in megacolon.

questions.text: Discuss the pharmacological effect of atropine on the CNS and eye and their clinical implications.
questions.explanation: Antimuscarinic CNS and ocular effects are both therapeutic and hazardous.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine causes central excitation and ocular mydriasis/cycloplegia with key risks.
questions.modelAnswer: CNS: at low doses minimal effects; at higher doses it causes restlessness, disorientation, confusion, hallucinations and even delirium and mania. Clinical implication: can be useful (e.g. in some Parkinsonian symptoms) but is often a dose-limiting adverse effect, especially in the elderly who are prone to delirium. Eye: causes mydriasis by paralysing the sphincter pupillae and cycloplegia by paralysing the ciliary muscle. Clinical implication: mydriasis is used for fundus examination, but in eyes with narrow anterior chambers it can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma; cycloplegia causes blurred near vision.

questions.text: Enumerate 4 adverse effects of cholinomimetics.
questions.explanation: Adverse effects mirror excess muscarinic stimulation across organ systems.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinomimetics cause GI, cardiac, respiratory and ocular muscarinic effects.
questions.modelAnswer: Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, increased salivation. Cardiovascular: bradycardia, hypotension, AV block. Respiratory: bronchospasm and increased bronchial secretions. Ocular: miosis, blurred vision, frontal headache. Genitourinary: urinary urgency and frequency.

questions.text: Enumerate the drugs which block cholinergic actions.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Antimuscarinics, neuromuscular and ganglion blockers, and botulinum toxin block cholinergic actions.
questions.modelAnswer: Cholinergic actions are blocked by antimuscarinic drugs, neuromuscular blockers, ganglion blockers and botulinum toxins.

questions.text: Enumerate the pharmacological actions of local eye application of atropine.
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks ocular muscarinic receptors, affecting pupil, lens and tears.
questions.keyConcept: Ocular atropine causes mydriasis, cycloplegia, raised IOP and dry eyes.
questions.modelAnswer: Mydriasis: pupil dilatation from blockade of M3 receptors on the sphincter pupillae muscle. Cycloplegia: paralysis of accommodation from blockade of M3 receptors on the ciliary muscle. Increased intraocular pressure: especially in narrow-angle glaucoma, by impairing aqueous humour outflow. Decreased lacrimation: reduced tear production leading to dry eyes.

questions.text: Enumerate the therapeutic uses of neostigmine.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Neostigmine treats myasthenia gravis and reverses curare-type blockade.
questions.modelAnswer: Neostigmine is used in myasthenia gravis and as an antidote to non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers such as curare.

questions.text: Enumerate the uses of hyoscine.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine treats motion sickness and is a preanesthetic in cardiac/thyrotoxic patients.
questions.modelAnswer: Hyoscine is used as a mydriatic, for the vomiting of motion sickness and Meniere's disease, and as a preanesthetic in thyrotoxic and cardiac patients.

questions.text: Enumerate two drugs that decrease acetylcholine release.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Aminoglycosides and botulinum toxin decrease acetylcholine release.
questions.modelAnswer: Acetylcholine release is decreased by aminoglycosides, botulinum toxins, and presynaptic M2 or alpha-2 agonists.

questions.text: Enumerate two drugs with atropine-like action.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: First-generation antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants have atropine-like effects.
questions.modelAnswer: Drugs with atropine-like (antimuscarinic) action include first-generation antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiarrhythmics, atropine substitutes and pethidine.

questions.text: Enumerate TWO indications of bethanechol.
questions.explanation: Bethanechol stimulates GIT and bladder smooth muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Bethanechol treats postoperative urine retention and paralytic ileus.
questions.modelAnswer: As a prokinetic agent it is used in megacolon, postoperative urinary retention, and postoperative paralytic ileus.

questions.text: Explain the mechanism of action of cholinesterase reactivators in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Oximes detach the organophosphate from cholinesterase, reactivating it.
questions.modelAnswer: Cholinesterase reactivators (oximes) reactivate the cholinesterase enzyme by binding to its anionic site and detaching the active organophosphate group from the enzyme via the free oxime.

questions.text: Explain why an enzyme reactivator should be used as early as possible during treatment of organophosphate toxicity.
questions.explanation: After ageing, the enzyme-organophosphate bond is irreversible and oximes fail.
questions.keyConcept: Oximes must be given before enzyme 'ageing' makes inhibition permanent.
questions.modelAnswer: Enzyme reactivators such as pralidoxime work by regenerating the acetylcholinesterase enzyme inhibited by organophosphates. If given early, before 'ageing' of the enzyme-organophosphate complex occurs, the reactivator can effectively restore enzyme function, which is particularly important for reversing nicotinic effects (muscle paralysis and respiratory failure). Delayed administration is far less effective because the aged complex is irreversible.

questions.text: Explain why atropine is used as preanesthetic medication.
questions.explanation: Antimuscarinic action dries secretions, protects the heart and limits vomiting.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine premedication dries secretions and prevents reflex bradycardia.
questions.modelAnswer: To reduce bronchial and salivary secretions: atropine blocks M3 receptors, preventing excessive secretions that could complicate anaesthesia and intubation. To prevent bradycardia and arrhythmias: it blocks cardiac M2 receptors, counteracting vagal reflexes and anaesthetic- or surgery-induced bradycardia. To decrease vomiting: it has antiemetic properties that reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting.

questions.text: Explain why atropine is used before neostigmine in the treatment of myasthenia gravis.
questions.explanation: Atropine pre-empts neostigmine's muscarinic excess.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine precedes neostigmine to block its muscarinic side effects.
questions.modelAnswer: Atropine is given to inhibit the muscarinic side effects of neostigmine, and it should precede neostigmine because neostigmine acts after a lag period and because atropine itself causes an initial bradycardia. Pre-treatment therefore blocks unwanted muscarinic effects (salivation, bradycardia, bronchospasm) while neostigmine's nicotinic effect strengthens muscle contraction.

questions.text: Explain why tropicamide is preferred to atropine in fundus examination of the elderly.
questions.explanation: Short action limits visual disturbance and glaucoma risk.
questions.keyConcept: Tropicamide's short action makes it safer for fundus exams in the elderly.
questions.modelAnswer: Tropicamide is preferred because it has a much shorter duration of action (4-6 hours) compared with atropine (days). This minimises prolonged visual impairment and reduces the risk of precipitating acute angle-closure glaucoma or worsening existing glaucoma in elderly patients, who are more susceptible.

questions.text: How is myasthenia gravis diagnosed pharmacologically?
questions.explanation: The short-acting anticholinesterase edrophonium confirms the diagnosis.
questions.keyConcept: Diagnose myasthenia gravis with the edrophonium test, EMG and anti-AChR antibodies.
questions.modelAnswer: Edrophonium (Tensilon) test (transient improvement in muscle strength), electromyography (EMG), and detection of anti-acetylcholine-receptor (anti-AChR) antibodies.

questions.text: Hyoscine is used as a preanesthetic in thyrotoxic and cardiac patients. Explain.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine is a pure antimuscarinic without initial bradycardia.
questions.modelAnswer: Hyoscine is a pure antagonist that does not cause the initial bradycardia seen with atropine, making it safer in thyrotoxic and cardiac patients.

questions.text: List 4 contraindications for using cholinomimetics.
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetics are avoided where increased cholinergic tone is harmful.
questions.keyConcept: Avoid cholinomimetics in asthma, ulcer, obstruction and cardiac disease.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronchial asthma/COPD: risk of severe bronchospasm. Peptic ulcer: risk of aggravation from increased gastric acid and motility. Intestinal/urinary obstruction: risk of rupture from increased smooth muscle contraction against an obstruction. Myocardial infarction/severe bradycardia: risk of worsening cardiac function. Hyperthyroidism: risk of atrial fibrillation from increased cardiac sensitivity.

questions.text: List 4 indications of atropine rather than atropine substitutes.
questions.explanation: These uses rely on atropine's broad central and peripheral antimuscarinic action.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine itself is used for OP poisoning, bradycardia, premedication and digoxin toxicity.
questions.modelAnswer: Organophosphate poisoning: acts on both central and peripheral muscarinic receptors. Bradyarrhythmia/AV block: increases heart rate by blocking cardiac M2 receptors. Preanesthetic medication: reduces secretions and prevents bradycardia. Digitalis toxicity: treats bradycardia or AV block induced by digoxin. Traveller's diarrhoea: reduces gastrointestinal motility and secretions.

questions.text: List the therapeutic uses of physostigmine.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Physostigmine treats glaucoma and reverses antimuscarinic (atropine) toxicity.
questions.modelAnswer: Physostigmine is used in glaucoma, as an antidote in atropine toxicity, and to counteract mydriatics after fundus examination.

questions.text: List three indications of pilocarpine.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocarpine is a miotic for glaucoma and a secretagogue for dry eye/mouth.
questions.modelAnswer: In the eye it is a miotic used to counteract mydriatics after fundus examination, to alternate with mydriatics in iridocyclitis to prevent synechiae, and in glaucoma. On exocrine glands it increases secretion and is used for dryness of the eye and mouth. On scalp blood vessels it causes vasodilation and is used as a hair tonic.

questions.text: List two adverse effects of hyoscine.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine causes sedation and amnesia but may cause excitement and hallucinations.
questions.modelAnswer: Hyoscine is more CNS depressant than atropine, causing drowsiness and amnesia, and when used as a preanesthetic (especially in females) it may induce CNS excitement, hallucinations and vivid dreams.

questions.text: List two causes of death in organophosphorus toxicity, mentioning the stimulated receptors.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Organophosphate death is from respiratory depression, muscle paralysis and pulmonary edema.
questions.modelAnswer: Death may result from respiratory center depression (M1 receptors), paralysis of the respiratory muscles due to persistent depolarization (Nm receptors), and excessive bronchial secretions with bronchospasm causing acute pulmonary edema (M3 receptors).

questions.text: Mention the mechanism of action of cevimeline and its use.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Cevimeline is a selective M3 agonist for dry eye/mouth in Sjogren syndrome.
questions.modelAnswer: Cevimeline is a selective M3 agonist used for dryness of the eye and mouth, for example in Sjogren syndrome.

questions.text: Mention the pharmacological effects of atropine on (a) the eye and (b) body secretions.
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors on ocular muscles and exocrine glands.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine dilates the pupil, paralyses accommodation and dries all secretions except milk.
questions.modelAnswer: Eye: long-acting mydriatic and cycloplegic, elevates intraocular pressure, and decreases lacrimation. Body secretions: decreases all body secretions (salivary, bronchial, sweat, gastric) except milk.

questions.text: Mention the pharmacological effects of atropine on body secretions.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine reduces all secretions except milk.
questions.modelAnswer: Atropine decreases lacrimation and reduces all body secretions except milk.

questions.text: Mention the possible adverse effects and toxicity of atropine.
questions.explanation: Atropine toxicity is the classic antimuscarinic toxidrome.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine toxicity: dry, hot, flushed, dilated, tachycardic and delirious.
questions.modelAnswer: Central nervous system: confusion, restlessness, hallucinations, delirium, hyperthermia. Ocular: blurred vision, photophobia, mydriasis, cycloplegia, acute glaucoma. Cardiovascular: tachycardia, palpitations. Gastrointestinal: dry mouth, constipation, decreased motility. Genitourinary: urinary retention. Skin: dry, hot, flushed skin ('red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as a pistol, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter').

questions.text: Mention two adverse effects of atropine.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine causes dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, hyperthermia and urine retention.
questions.modelAnswer: Atropine can cause CNS effects (confusion, hallucination, delirium), eye effects (blurred vision, photophobia, sandy eye), dry mouth and skin, tachycardia, hyperthermia, flushing, urine retention in older men and constipation.

questions.text: Mention two causes of toxicity of organophosphorus compounds.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Organophosphate toxicity arises from suicide, insecticide exposure and nerve gases.
questions.modelAnswer: Causes include suicide, accidental exposure while spraying insecticides (parathion, malathion) and exposure to nerve gases (such as sarin) during war.

questions.text: Outline the lines of treatment of atropine toxicity.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine toxicity is treated with physostigmine, diazepam and cooling.
questions.modelAnswer: Treatment includes gastric lavage, physostigmine (which antagonizes the central and peripheral effects), diazepam to control CNS excitement and cooling blankets to treat hyperthermia in children.

questions.text: Outline the treatment of atropine toxicity.
questions.explanation: Physostigmine is the specific antidote because it crosses into the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine toxicity is treated supportively plus physostigmine.
questions.modelAnswer: Supportive care: maintain airway, breathing and circulation; control hyperthermia with cooling (especially in children). Gastric lavage: if ingestion is recent. Physostigmine: given intravenously, as it is a tertiary amine that crosses the BBB and antagonises both central and peripheral muscarinic effects. Diazepam: for seizures or severe CNS excitement.

questions.text: Outline the treatment of organophosphate poisoning.
questions.explanation: Treatment combines decontamination, atropine, an oxime reactivator and seizure control.
questions.keyConcept: Manage organophosphate poisoning with atropine, pralidoxime and supportive care.
questions.modelAnswer: Emergency management: secure airway, breathing and circulation; remove contaminated clothing and wash the skin. Atropine: given intravenously to counteract muscarinic effects (bradycardia, secretions, bronchospasm), titrated until muscarinic signs disappear. Pralidoxime (2-PAM): given intravenously as an enzyme reactivator to regenerate acetylcholinesterase, especially effective for nicotinic effects (muscle weakness). Diazepam: for seizures or central nervous system excitation.

questions.text: Pyridostigmine is preferred to neostigmine in myasthenia gravis. Explain.
questions.explanation: Review the related lecture material for the rationale.
questions.keyConcept: Pyridostigmine is longer acting with fewer GIT effects than neostigmine.
questions.modelAnswer: Pyridostigmine has a longer duration of action (better compliance), fewer visceral (GIT) side effects and is more selective on skeletal muscle.

questions.text: What are the disadvantages of acetylcholine if it were used as a systemic drug?
questions.explanation: Its non-selectivity and rapid breakdown make systemic ACh impractical.
questions.keyConcept: Systemic ACh is non-selective, poorly absorbed and rapidly hydrolysed.
questions.modelAnswer: Acetylcholine lacks specificity (it acts on all cholinergic receptors), is irregularly absorbed (being a quaternary compound), and is rapidly hydrolysed by cholinesterase if given systemically, giving it no useful duration of action.

questions.text: Cross match each atropine substitute to its use.
questions.explanation: Hyoscine butylbromide relieves GI/biliary spasm; benztropine is a central antimuscarinic for parkinsonism; oxybutynin relaxes the detrusor; glycopyrrolate dries secretions preoperatively; homatropine provides cycloplegia for iridocyclitis.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine substitutes are chosen for organ-selective antimuscarinic uses.

pairs.target: Antispasmodic
Anti-parkinsonian
Urinary incontinence
Preanesthetic medication
Iridocyclitis (cycloplegia)

questions.text: Cross match each cholinomimetic drug to its therapeutic indication.
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine (direct muscarinic agonist) for glaucoma/dry mouth; bethanechol stimulates bladder/bowel; neostigmine (quaternary anticholinesterase) reverses curare and treats myasthenia; physostigmine (tertiary, crosses BBB) reverses central anticholinergic toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Indications of direct and indirect cholinomimetics.

pairs.target: Glaucoma / miotic / xerostomia
Megacolon and postoperative urinary retention
Antidote for curare and treatment of myasthenia gravis
Atropine (anticholinergic) toxicity

questions.text: Cross match each neuromuscular blocker to its elimination-related feature.
questions.explanation: Mivacurium is metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase; atracurium undergoes organ-independent Hofmann elimination; vecuronium is mainly hepatic (avoid in liver disease); pancuronium is renally excreted (avoid in renal failure).
questions.keyConcept: Elimination route determines NMB choice in organ dysfunction.

pairs.target: Hydrolyzed by pseudocholinesterase
May be given in renal or liver disease (Hofmann elimination)
May be given in renal but not in liver disease
Avoided in renal disease

questions.text: Cross match each neuromuscular blocker to its most suitable cardiac-related feature.
questions.explanation: Mivacurium is shortest-acting (plasma cholinesterase); vecuronium is cardiovascularly stable; pancuronium causes vagolytic tachycardia; rocuronium has rapid onset for rapid-sequence intubation.
questions.keyConcept: Cardiac safety profiles of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers.

pairs.target: Shortest-acting non-depolarizing blocker
Preferred in cardiac patients (cardiostable)
Avoided in cardiac patients (vagolytic tachycardia)
Alternative to succinylcholine for rapid endotracheal intubation

questions.text: Cross match each spasmolytic drug to its mechanism and use.
questions.explanation: Diazepam enhances GABA-A; baclofen is a GABA-B agonist; tizanidine is a central α2 agonist; dantrolene blocks Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is the antidote for malignant hyperthermia.
questions.keyConcept: Spasmolytics act centrally (GABA-A/B, α2) or directly on skeletal muscle (dantrolene).

pairs.target: GABA-A agonist; used in most causes of spasticity
GABA-B agonist; used in multiple sclerosis
α2 agonist; used in multiple sclerosis
Acts on skeletal muscle (ryanodine receptor); used in malignant hyperthermia

questions.text: Match each cholinergic drug with the appropriate description.
questions.explanation: Edrophonium acts very briefly; physostigmine is a tertiary amine acting centrally and peripherally; pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme after organophosphate poisoning; neostigmine also directly stimulates neuromuscular nicotinic receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Anticholinesterases differ in duration, CNS access and direct receptor action.

pairs.target: Inhibition of cholinesterase is very short (2-10 minutes)
Inhibits cholinesterase in the periphery as well as in the central nervous system
Regenerates cholinesterase blocked by organophosphates
Inhibits cholinesterase and directly activates Nm cholinergic receptors

questions.text: Match each drug to the statement that best describes it.
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine is hydrolyzed by pseudocholinesterase; atropine worsens urinary retention in BPH; edrophonium is a short-acting anticholinesterase; pilocarpine is a direct muscarinic agonist for glaucoma; sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium (no atropine needed); gantacurium is inactivated by cysteine and reversible by neostigmine.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinergic drugs differ by metabolism, reversal, and clinical use.

pairs.premise: Rapidly hydrolyzed in liver and plasma by esterases
pairs.target: Succinylcholine

pairs.premise: Relatively contraindicated in benign prostatic hypertrophy
pairs.target: Atropine

pairs.premise: Exerts its effects via inhibition of acetylcholinesterase
pairs.target: Edrophonium

pairs.premise: Useful in glaucoma by activating muscarinic receptors in the eye
pairs.target: Pilocarpine

pairs.premise: Reverses rocuronium-induced blockade and is not preceded by atropine
pairs.target: Sugammadex

pairs.premise: Its neuromuscular block may be reversed by neostigmine or cysteine
pairs.target: Gantacurium

questions.text: A 6-year-old boy became unconscious 2 hours after eating an apple from a local vendor. He was salivating profusely, incontinent of urine and faeces, with pinpoint pupils, moist skin and shallow respiration. Which pair of drugs was most likely given intravenously?
questions.explanation: The cholinergic crisis indicates organophosphate poisoning, treated with atropine (to block muscarinic effects) and pralidoxime (to reactivate cholinesterase).
questions.keyConcept: Organophosphate poisoning is treated with atropine plus pralidoxime.

questions.text: A 61-year-old man with long-standing open-angle glaucoma developed brow ache, difficulty with far vision and trouble seeing in dim light one month after changing his ophthalmic medication. Which was most likely his new drug?
questions.explanation: Physostigmine is an indirect cholinomimetic that lowers intraocular pressure by increasing aqueous humour outflow; its miosis and ciliary spasm cause brow ache and poor dim-light vision.
questions.keyConcept: Anticholinesterase miotics cause brow ache and dim-light difficulty.

questions.text: A 62-year-old woman had no bowel movements 4 days after surgery to remove colon cancer. Adynamic ileus was diagnosed and intramuscular neostigmine was given. Activation of which receptor most likely mediated the therapeutic effect?
questions.explanation: Neostigmine raises acetylcholine, which acts on M3 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract to promote motility in adynamic ileus.
questions.keyConcept: GIT motility is driven by M3 receptor activation.

questions.text: A 74-year-old man reported worsening memory, difficulty recognising familiar objects and trouble planning daily activities, and was diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Which drug would most likely be prescribed?
questions.explanation: Donepezil is a central acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that raises brain acetylcholine to treat the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease.
questions.keyConcept: Donepezil is a central anticholinesterase used in Alzheimer's disease.

questions.text: A clinically useful drug that acts by decreasing acetylcholine release is:
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin inhibits acetylcholine release from nerve terminals; atropine blocks receptors and curare blocks the nicotinic receptor.
questions.keyConcept: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release.

questions.text: A medication that triggers malignant hyperthermia in susceptible individuals is:
questions.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anesthetics (halothane) and by succinylcholine in genetically susceptible individuals (ryanodine receptor mutation). Non-depolarizing blockers (rocuronium, atracurium) are safe.
questions.keyConcept: Halothane and succinylcholine are the classic triggers of malignant hyperthermia.

questions.text: A patient presents to the ER with rhinorrhea, salivation, confusion, lacrimation, urinary and fecal incontinence, bradycardia, muscle fasciculations and seizures. Which agent is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: This cholinergic crisis (SLUDGE plus fasciculations and CNS effects) is typical of organophosphate poisoning; malathion is an organophosphate cholinesterase inhibitor. Atropine and scopolamine are antimuscarinics (opposite picture), and pralidoxime is part of treatment.
questions.keyConcept: Organophosphates (e.g., malathion) cause a cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE + fasciculations).

questions.text: Activation of muscarinic receptors does not result in:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic activation contracts the iris sphincter causing miosis (pupil constriction), not dilation.
questions.keyConcept: Muscarinic activation causes miosis, not mydriasis.
options: Dilation of the pupils due to relaxation of the iris sphincter
Contraction of the detrusor muscle of the bladder
Decreased conduction velocity through the AV node

questions.text: Activation of muscarinic receptors does not result in:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic activation contracts the sphincter pupillae causing miosis, not pupil dilatation.
questions.keyConcept: Muscarinic activation causes miosis, not mydriasis.
options: Dilatation of the pupils due to relaxation of the sphincter muscle of the iris
Contraction of the detrusor muscle of the bladder
Decreased conduction velocity through the AV node

questions.text: Activation of muscarinic receptors results in:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic activation stimulates the constrictor pupillae muscle, producing miosis.
questions.keyConcept: Muscarinic activation causes miosis.
options: Increased conduction velocity through the AV node
Miosis due to stimulation of the constrictor pupillae muscle

questions.text: All of the following are effects of a selective M3 agonist except:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic activation slows the heart (via M2), so increasing heart rate is not an M3-agonist effect.
questions.keyConcept: Muscarinic agonists slow the heart.

questions.text: All of the following drugs are used to counteract mydriatics after fundus examination except:
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine, physostigmine and ecothiopate are cholinomimetics that cause miosis; hyoscine is an anticholinergic that causes mydriasis.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine dilates, so it cannot reverse a mydriatic.

questions.text: All the following are contraindications to succinylcholine EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine is actually used during electroconvulsive therapy to prevent injury. It is contraindicated in muscle trauma, burns and crush injuries (hyperkalemia risk) and in malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
questions.keyConcept: Succinylcholine is contraindicated where hyperkalemia or malignant hyperthermia is a risk; it is used in ECT.

questions.text: All the following are effects of Cevimeline (M3 selective agonist) except:
questions.explanation: Cevimeline stimulates glandular secretion and causes vasodilatation; it does not directly increase heart rate.
questions.keyConcept: M3 agonists do not directly raise heart rate.

questions.text: All the following drugs have significant nicotinic actions except:
questions.explanation: Bethanechol is a pure muscarinic agonist with minimal nicotinic action.
questions.keyConcept: Bethanechol is selectively muscarinic.

questions.text: An atropine substitute for treatment of urinary incontinence:
questions.explanation: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic that relaxes the detrusor and is used for urinary incontinence/overactive bladder.
questions.keyConcept: Oxybutynin treats urinary incontinence.

questions.text: At the end of an operation, the action of a neuromuscular blocker is reversed by:
questions.explanation: Non-depolarizing blockade is reversed with neostigmine, preceded by atropine/glycopyrrolate to prevent neostigmine muscarinic effects (bradycardia, secretions).
questions.keyConcept: Reverse non-depolarizing block with neostigmine, giving atropine first to block muscarinic effects.

questions.text: Atropine does not:
questions.explanation: Atropine reduces secretions and smooth muscle tone but does not lower blood pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine does not reduce blood pressure.
options: Reduce tone and motility of the GIT

questions.text: Atropine does not antagonize the following feature of anticholinesterase poisoning:
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks only muscarinic effects; the nicotinic neuromuscular paralysis requires an oxime (pralidoxime), so atropine cannot reverse it.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine does not reverse nicotinic muscle paralysis.

questions.text: Atropine is combined with anticholinesterases in myasthenia gravis to:
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks the unwanted muscarinic effects (salivation, bradycardia, GI cramps) while leaving the desired nicotinic effect at the neuromuscular junction.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine blocks muscarinic side effects of anticholinesterases.

questions.text: Atropine is used as a pre-anesthetic because of all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Atropine does not lower blood pressure (it tends to raise heart rate); its pre-anesthetic value lies in vagal block, antiemesis and drying/bronchodilation.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine does not decrease blood pressure.
options: To induce bronchodilation and stimulate respiration

questions.text: Atropine is used as a preanesthetic because of all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors and does not decrease blood pressure; it can even cause tachycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine does not lower blood pressure as a preanesthetic.
options: To induce bronchodilatation and stimulate respiration

questions.text: Atropine is used as preanesthetic medication due to all the following except:
questions.explanation: Atropine causes tachycardia by blocking cardiac M2 receptors and does not decrease blood pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine does not lower blood pressure.
options: It blocks cardiac muscarinic receptors and decreases risk of cardiac arrest
It induces bronchodilation and stimulates respiration

questions.text: Atropine is used in the treatment of:
questions.explanation: Malathion is an organophosphate; atropine antagonizes its muscarinic effects and is a mainstay of treatment.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine treats organophosphate (malathion) toxicity.

questions.text: Atropine itself, not its substitutes, can be used in:
questions.explanation: Atropine acts on central and peripheral muscarinic receptors, making it the agent used in organophosphate (Malathion) poisoning.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine is the antimuscarinic used in organophosphate poisoning.

questions.text: Atropine substitutes used as mydriatic cycloplegic (Homatropine) are preferred to atropine because they are:
questions.explanation: Homatropine has a shorter duration of action and its mydriatic effect is more easily reversed than atropine's (B and C).
questions.keyConcept: Synthetic cycloplegics are shorter-acting and easily reversed.

questions.text: Atropine substitutes used as mydriatic cycloplegics are preferred over atropine because they are:
questions.explanation: Synthetic agents have a shorter duration and are easily reversed by a cholinomimetic, making them more convenient than long-acting atropine.
questions.keyConcept: Synthetic mydriatics are shorter-acting and reversible.

questions.text: Atropine toxicity includes:
questions.explanation: Antimuscarinic toxicity causes urinary retention (plus dry mouth, hot flushed skin and constipation), not salivation or diarrhea.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine causes urinary retention.

questions.text: Competitive neuromuscular blocker(s) used for endotracheal intubation is/are:
questions.explanation: Gantacurium (ultra-short non-depolarizer) and rocuronium (rapid-onset non-depolarizer) are competitive blockers used for intubation. Succinylcholine is a depolarizing (non-competitive) blocker.
questions.keyConcept: Gantacurium and rocuronium are competitive blockers suitable for intubation.

questions.text: Fasciculations produced by succinylcholine do not induce:
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine-induced fasciculations cause hyperkalemia (not hypokalemia) from muscle depolarization, along with postoperative myalgia, raised intragastric/intraocular pressure, and aspiration risk.
questions.keyConcept: Succinylcholine causes hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia.

questions.text: Hyoscine differs from atropine in all the following except:
questions.explanation: Hyoscine is a shorter-acting mydriatic than atropine, so claiming it is longer-acting is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine is a shorter-acting mydriatic than atropine.
options: Pure antagonist thus induces initial bradycardia

questions.text: Hyoscine differs from atropine in all the following except:
questions.explanation: Atropine is a longer-acting mydriatic than hyoscine, so this is not a way hyoscine differs.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine is a shorter-acting mydriatic than atropine.
options: Pure antagonist thus does not induce initial bradycardia

questions.text: Hyoscine differs from atropine in that it:
questions.explanation: Hyoscine has greater central depressant effects (drowsiness, amnesia) than atropine.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine is more CNS-depressant than atropine.
options: Has a longer duration of action
Has more central CNS depressant effects
Has a more potent effect on the heart than atropine
Has a weaker effect in motion sickness

questions.text: Hyoscine produces all the following actions except:
questions.explanation: Hyoscine causes passive mydriasis with cycloplegia, not active mydriasis.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine causes passive, not active, mydriasis.

questions.text: Local administration of cholinomimetics in the eye does not induce:
questions.explanation: Topical cholinomimetics cause miosis with lacrimation, lid twitching and congestion; the resulting small pupil increases depth of focus rather than blurring vision.
questions.keyConcept: Miosis improves depth of focus rather than blurring vision.

questions.text: Local administration of cholinomimetics in the eye does not induce:
questions.explanation: Local cholinomimetics cause miosis, lacrimation, ciliary contraction and conjunctival congestion; per the source key, the marked answer here is blurring of vision (they do not dilate the pupil).
questions.keyConcept: Ocular cholinomimetics cause miosis and ciliary spasm, not dilatation.

questions.text: Neostigmine:
questions.explanation: As a cholinomimetic, neostigmine can provoke bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma; it antagonizes curare and raises (not lowers) acetylcholine.
questions.keyConcept: Neostigmine is contraindicated in asthma.
options: Decreases acetylcholine level at the motor end plate
Has a shorter duration than edrophonium

questions.text: Neostigmine:
questions.explanation: Neostigmine increases acetylcholine and can cause bronchoconstriction, so it is contraindicated in bronchial asthma.
questions.keyConcept: Neostigmine is contraindicated in asthma.
options: Decreases acetylcholine level at the motor end plate
Has a shorter duration than edrophonium

questions.text: Neuromuscular blocker(s) used for endotracheal intubation is/are:
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine (ultra-short, rapid onset) and rocuronium (rapid-onset non-depolarizer) provide rapid intubating conditions. Pancuronium has too slow an onset.
questions.keyConcept: Succinylcholine and rocuronium provide rapid intubating conditions.

questions.text: Organophosphorus toxicity is characterised by all the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Organophosphate toxicity causes miosis (pinpoint pupils) from muscarinic overstimulation, not mydriasis.
questions.keyConcept: Organophosphate poisoning causes miosis, not mydriasis.

questions.text: Organophosphorus toxicity is characterized by all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Organophosphate poisoning causes miosis (pinpoint pupils), not mydriasis, so mydriasis is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Organophosphate poisoning causes miosis, not mydriasis.

questions.text: Pilocarpine:
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist that causes miosis and ciliary contraction, improving aqueous outflow and lowering intraocular pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocarpine lowers intraocular pressure.
options: Is used to lower intraocular pressure

questions.text: Pyridostigmine is the drug of choice in treatment of:
questions.explanation: Pyridostigmine is a quaternary anticholinesterase with a longer duration than neostigmine, making it the maintenance drug of choice in myasthenia gravis. Central anticholinesterases (donepezil) treat Alzheimer disease, and physostigmine treats atropine toxicity.
questions.keyConcept: Pyridostigmine is the maintenance anticholinesterase of choice in myasthenia gravis.

questions.text: Regarding neostigmine, which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation: Neostigmine is given after atropine pre-treatment so that its muscarinic effects are blocked while its neuromuscular nicotinic action is used.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine pre-treatment blocks neostigmine's muscarinic effects.
options: Quaternary amine and cannot cross BBB
Preceded by atropine to block muscarinic effects

questions.text: Regarding neostigmine, which of the following is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Because neostigmine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, physostigmine (a tertiary amine) is the antidote for central atropine toxicity, so this statement is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Physostigmine, not neostigmine, treats atropine toxicity.
options: Quaternary amine and cannot cross the BBB
Preceded by atropine to block unwanted muscarinic effects

questions.text: Regarding precautions and contraindications of cholinomimetics:
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetics should not be given IV and are contraindicated with obstruction, peptic ulcer or asthma, so all precautions apply.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinomimetics have multiple key contraindications.
options: Never given in the presence of urinary or intestinal obstruction
Never given in the presence of peptic ulcer or bronchial asthma

questions.text: Regarding the management of succinylcholine apnea, which is CORRECT?
questions.explanation: Prolonged succinylcholine apnea that has progressed to a phase II (desensitizing) block resembles a non-depolarizing block and can be reversed with neostigmine, preceded by atropine to block muscarinic effects. Neostigmine worsens a phase I block.
questions.keyConcept: Phase II succinylcholine block can be reversed with neostigmine (after atropine).
options: Dantrolene preceded by atropine in phase II block
Neostigmine preceded by atropine in phase I block
Neostigmine preceded by atropine in phase II block
Physostigmine preceded by atropine in phase II block

questions.text: Synthetic mydriatic cycloplegics differ from atropine in the following except:
questions.explanation: Atropine remains the preferred cycloplegic for refraction in children due to its complete effect, so synthetic agents being preferred in children is not a true difference.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine is preferred for cycloplegic refraction in children.
options: Their mydriatic action is easier to reverse
Used alternating with miotics in iridocyclitis

questions.text: Synthetic mydriatic cycloplegics (e.g. Homatropine) differ from atropine in all the following except:
questions.explanation: Both atropine and its synthetic substitutes are used alternating with miotics in iridocyclitis, so this is not a difference.
questions.keyConcept: Alternating with miotics is shared, not a distinguishing feature.
options: Their mydriatic action is easier to reverse
Used alternating with miotics in iridocyclitis

questions.text: The cause of death in organophosphorus poisoning is:
questions.explanation: Death results from respiratory failure due to bronchospasm, bronchial secretions and paralysis of respiratory muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Organophosphate poisoning kills by respiratory failure.

questions.text: The following are therapeutic uses of atropine rather than atropine substitutes except:
questions.explanation: Asthma and COPD are treated with the inhaled atropine substitute ipratropium, not atropine itself, so this is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Asthma/COPD use ipratropium, not atropine.

questions.text: The following are therapeutic uses of atropine rather than atropine substitutes except:
questions.explanation: Asthma and COPD are managed with atropine substitutes such as ipratropium, not atropine itself.
questions.keyConcept: Inhaled antimuscarinic substitutes, not atropine, treat asthma/COPD.

questions.text: The following drugs are matched to their indications except:
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetics are contraindicated in megacolon; neostigmine is used for paralytic ileus, not megacolon, so this match is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Neostigmine is contraindicated in megacolon.
options: Bethanechol / postoperative urine retention and paralytic ileus

questions.text: The following drugs are used to counteract mydriatics after fundus examination except:
questions.explanation: Hyoscine is itself an antimuscarinic mydriatic and cannot reverse mydriasis; the cholinomimetic miotics do.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine is a mydriatic, not a reversal agent.

questions.text: The following is a contraindication to the use of cholinomimetics:
questions.explanation: Per the source key, postoperative abdominal distension is taken as the answer, since it is actually an indication for cholinomimetics; the other options are genuine contraindications.
questions.keyConcept: Postoperative distension is an indication, not contraindication.

questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about carbamates:
questions.explanation: Neostigmine is a reversible (carbamate) cholinesterase inhibitor; the irreversible inhibitors are the organophosphates, so this statement is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Neostigmine is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor.
options: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine used to counteract central and peripheral atropine toxicity
Neostigmine is a quaternary amine used as an antidote to neuromuscular blockers
Neostigmine is a synthetic irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor
Pyridostigmine is a neostigmine analogue used in myasthenia gravis

questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about carbamates:
questions.explanation: Neostigmine is a reversible cholinesterase inhibitor, not irreversible, so this statement is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamates like neostigmine are reversible anticholinesterases.
options: Physostigmine is a tertiary amine used to counteract atropine toxicity centrally and peripherally
Neostigmine is a quaternary amine that can be used as an antidote to neuromuscular blockers
Neostigmine is a synthetic irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor
Pyridostigmine is a neostigmine analogue used in myasthenia gravis

questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about hyoscine:
questions.explanation: Atropine is a longer-acting mydriatic than hyoscine, so describing hyoscine as longer-acting is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Hyoscine is a shorter-acting mydriatic than atropine.
options: Induces drowsiness and amnesia more than atropine
May induce CNS excitement and vivid dreams
Pure antagonist without initial bradycardia, so preferred to atropine in thyrotoxic and cardiac patients

questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about pilocarpine:
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine is a miotic, not a mydriatic cycloplegic, so it is not used to dilate the pupil for fundus examination.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocarpine is a miotic, not a mydriatic.
options: Tertiary amine with a pure M3 agonistic effect
Used alternating with atropine in iridocyclitis to prevent synechiae
Preferred over physostigmine in the treatment of glaucoma
Used in fundus examination as a mydriatic cycloplegic

questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about pilocarpine:
questions.explanation: Pilocarpine is a miotic that lowers intraocular pressure; it is not a mydriatic for fundus examination.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocarpine is a miotic, not a mydriatic.
options: Tertiary with pure M3 agonistic effect
Used alternating with atropine in iridocyclitis to prevent synechia
Preferred to physostigmine in treatment of glaucoma
Used in fundus examination as a mydriatic cycloplegic

questions.text: The following is an incorrect statement about bethanechol:
questions.explanation: Bethanechol is a quaternary compound with low lipid solubility that does not cross the BBB, so it lacks central adverse effects.
questions.keyConcept: Bethanechol does not cause central effects.
options: Has low lipid solubility and is not hydrolyzed by cholinesterase
Has a marked muscarinic effect especially on the GIT and bladder
Has a prokinetic effect, so it is used in megacolon and urine retention
Has central adverse effects such as irritability and respiratory depression

questions.text: The following is an incorrect statement about bethanechol:
questions.explanation: Bethanechol is a quaternary amine that does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it lacks central adverse effects.
questions.keyConcept: Bethanechol has no central effects (it does not cross the BBB).
options: Has low lipid solubility and is not hydrolysed by cholinesterase enzyme
Has marked muscarinic effect especially on the GIT and bladder
Has prokinetic effect, so used in megacolon and urine retention
Has central adverse effects in the form of irritability and respiratory depression

questions.text: The following is incorrect about cholinomimetics:
questions.explanation: Atropine is combined with neostigmine to block muscarinic effects in conditions such as myasthenia gravis, but it is not specifically added before neostigmine for postoperative urine retention in this sense.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine pre-treatment is not part of treating urine retention with neostigmine.
options: Pyridostigmine is preferred in myasthenia gravis
Atropine is added before neostigmine in treatment of postoperative urine retention
Physostigmine is used in treatment of atropine toxicity

questions.text: The following is not a contraindication to the use of cholinomimetics:
questions.explanation: Postoperative abdominal distension is actually an indication for prokinetic cholinomimetics, not a contraindication.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinomimetics treat postoperative distension.

questions.text: The following is not an action of cholinomimetics on the heart:
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetics slow AV nodal conduction and shorten the atrial refractory period, but they do not decrease atrial muscle conduction in this sense.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinergic cardiac effects mainly slow rate and AV conduction.
options: Decrease heart rate and conduction at the atrioventricular node

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of atropine:
questions.explanation: Atropine reduces sweating, so marked sweating is not an adverse effect; it causes dry, hot skin.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine reduces sweating (causing hot, dry skin).
options: Retention of urine in patients with enlarged prostate

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of atropine:
questions.explanation: Atropine causes tachycardia through muscarinic blockade; bradycardia is not an expected adverse effect.
questions.keyConcept: Atropine causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of cholinomimetic eye drops:
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetic eye drops lower intraocular pressure and treat glaucoma rather than cause it.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinomimetics treat, not cause, glaucoma.

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of cholinomimetics:
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetics slow the heart (bradycardia) via muscarinic action, so tachycardia is not an adverse effect.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinomimetics cause bradycardia, not tachycardia.

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of cholinomimetics:
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetics cause bradycardia through muscarinic stimulation of the heart, not tachycardia.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinomimetics cause bradycardia, not tachycardia.

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of cholinomimetics:
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetics cause hypotension through vasodilatation, not hypertension.
questions.keyConcept: Cholinomimetics cause hypotension, not hypertension.

questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of the cholinomimetic:
questions.explanation: Cholinomimetics lower intraocular pressure, so glaucoma is an indication for them, not an adverse effect.
questions.keyConcept: Glaucoma is an indication, not an adverse effect, of cholinomimetics.

questions.text: The following is not an indication for using neostigmine:
